title: Evaluation of Economic and Health Outcomes Associated With Food Taxes and Subsidies
abstract: Importance: Fiscal policy is a promising approach to incentivizing better food choices and reducing the burden of chronic disease. To inform guidelines on using fiscal policies, including taxes and subsidies, to promote health, the World Health Organization commissioned a systematic review and meta-analysis of the worldwide literature on the outcomes of such policies for food products. Objective: To assess the outcomes of implemented food taxes and subsidies for prices, sales, consumption, and population-level diet and health. Data Sources: Eight bibliographic databases were searched for peer-reviewed literature and 14 data sources along with governmental websites were searched for grey literature that were published from database inception through June 1, 2020. There were no language and setting restrictions. Study Selection: Only primary studies of implemented food taxes and subsidies were considered for inclusion. Data Extraction and Synthesis: The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) reporting guideline was followed. A 3-level random-effects model was used to conduct a meta-analysis of sales and consumption outcomes of fruit and vegetable subsidies. Other outcomes were analyzed in a narrative synthesis. Main Outcomes and Measures: Study estimates in the meta-analysis were combined using a price elasticity measure for sales and consumption outcomes. Heterogeneity was assessed using the I2 statistic and τ2. Studies varied in how diet and health were measured. Results: A total of 54 articles were included in the systematic review, of which 15 studies were included in the meta-analysis. Most food subsidies targeted fruits and vegetables and populations with low income, whereas the evidence on food taxes was primarily from the nonessential energy-dense food tax in Mexico. Sales of subsidized fruits and vegetables increased significantly, with an estimated price elasticity of demand of -0.59 (95% CI, -1.04 to -0.13 [P = .02]; 95% prediction interval, -2.07 to 0.90; I2 = 92.4% [95% CI, 89.0%-94.8%; P < .001]), suggesting inelastic demand. There was no significant change in the consumption of subsidized fruits and vegetables, with an estimated price elasticity of demand of -0.17 (95% CI, -0.49 to 0.15 [P = .26]; 95% prediction interval, -1.01 to 0.67; I2 = 76.2% [95% CI, 54.3%-87.6%; P < .001]). Food excise taxes were associated with higher prices and reduced sales. Evidence was limited on the differential outcomes of food taxes and subsidies across subpopulations. Conclusions and Relevance: Results of this systematic review and meta-analysis indicated that fruit and vegetable subsidies were associated with a moderate increase in fruit and vegetable sales. Further research is warranted to understand the implications of food taxes and subsidies for population-level consumption, diet, and health outcomes.

title: Muddling Through the Inflation
abstract: This chapter discusses how to deal with inflation, focusing on the US and Eurozone inflation, inflationary effect on emerging developing countries (EDCs) along with China, Asia and other Asia. Inflation rises steadily in the US, with cost of living rising more than forecast in February 2011, led by the highest food prices since 2008 and rising fuel costs. Since then, the world is confronted with new uncertainties, spreading unrest in the Middle East and worse-than-expected effects of Japanese earthquake or tsunami in the face of robust global growth in manufacturing. The eurozone is similarly impacted. Factory gate prices in February 2011 posted their sharpest annual gain (12.8 percent) in nearly two and half years, putting pressure on the European Central Bank (ECB) to raise interest rates soon. Inflation is much more serious in the EDCs, especially the BRIICs (Brazil, Russia, India, Indonesia, and China). The fight against inflation is already weighing in on EDCs, from China to India, South Korea, to Indonesia. In Asia, inflation is expected to exceed 5 percent in 2011. Chinese inflation remained stubbornly high at 4.9 percent in February 2011, surpassing the government's target of 4 percent. The biggest risk is a rerun of 1970s stagflation, if monetary conditions continue to stroke demand, while supply remains tight reflecting decades of underinvestment, monopolies in extractive industries, mounting unrest in key commodity producers, and rising inflationary expectations.

title: Plant Disease Detection Using Machine Learning Tools With an Overview on Dimensionality Reduction
abstract: Food security is a matter of concern for different countries, irrespective of their developmental status. Plant stress response is one of the major concerns for crop productivity. “Climate change and global warming turned out to be the main contributors to crop loss by imparting both abiotic and biotic stress to the plant. Identifying the reasons and solutions to the problems related to crop loss is one of the major areas of concentration for researchers worldwide. The traditional method of identification, classification and quantification of plant stress by visual phenotyping needs specialized human resources and is often associated with erroneous results. An array of different parameters contributes significantly to the decrease in crop yield. Machine Learning (ML) has revolutionized the way in which we approach and deal with such problems nowadays, i.e., predicting the outcome with a reliable accuracy score, thus preventing the crop loss significantly. Researches concerned with Plant Stress Biology (PSB) have gained significant impetus due to the advent of ML techniques, where prediction studies can be carried out based on the feature space for both image and numeric datasets. This feature space is generally large, owing to the correlation between different features with the final outcome for classification. In this book chapter, we have particularly aimed towards introducing the concept of Dimensionality Reduction and have dealt with the part of “Feature Extraction” in particular. Dimensionality Reduction is a part of data pre- processing and is focused on reducing the original feature space by getting rid of the redundant and less important attributes. Our chapter will focus on the understanding the different feature extraction techniques for both numeric and image data for effective prediction of plant disease as a result of biotic stress. We will also focus on the implementation of some of these techniques on publicly available datasets to understand how the dimensionality reduction methods work to provide us with reliable outcomes for prediction of crop diseases and assist in their management.

title: Crop Breeding for Climate Resilience: Integrating Genomics and Phenomics with Bioinformatics
abstract: As the global climate undergoes unprecedented shifts, ensuring food security demands innovative approaches that bolster crop resilience. The complex environment of contemporary agricultural advances, where the fusion of genetics, phenomics, and bioinformatics emerges as a transformational force. Genomic insights illuminate the genetic basis of stress tolerance, while high-throughput phenotyping offers a dynamic portrayal of plant responses. Bioinformatics, the linchpin of this integration, empowers us to decipher complex data and predict trait performance. To successfully bridge the gap between research and practical application, it is essential to combine genomic and phenomic data within comprehensive databases and platforms tailored to specific plant groups. These platforms should also incorporate user-friendly tools that empower breeders to make informed conclusions concerning the selection of traits that enhance climate adaptability. This chapter meticulously details these components, expounding on genomic sequencing, marker-assisted selection, remote sensing, imaging techniques, data integration, pathway analysis, and machine learning. Challenges, encompassing ethics, environmental impacts, and field validation, are scrutinized, underscoring the balanced progression required. In conclusion, the chapter paints a comprehensive portrait of an integrated approach that redefines the future of agriculture, galvanizing climate-resilient crop breeding to tackle the multifaceted challenges of our era.

title: Prediction of Traits Using Artificial Intelligence Machine Learning
abstract: Geopolitical instabilities, climate fluctuations, and the COVID-19 pandemic have underscored the vulnerabilities within global food systems, intensifying the imperative to address food security challenges. With the global population projected to reach 10 billion by 2050 and food demand expected to surge by 70%, urgent attention is needed to bolster food production. In this context, the fusion of artificial intelligence (AI) and genomic technologies offers a revolutionary potential for agriculture. Genomic sequencing techniques have rapidly expanded plant genomic resources, facilitating a deeper understanding of genetic variations crucial for enhancing crop resilience and productivity. Leveraging genotyping methods such as genome resequencing and single nucleotide polymorphism arrays has enabled the identification of genetic markers associated with desirable agronomic traits. Additionally, using plant pangenomes as references provides a deeper understanding of genomic diversity, which helps in developing crops with better disease resistance and stress tolerance. In parallel, the adoption of AI, particularly machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) algorithms, has revolutionized agriculture by optimizing crop breeding and management processes. These advanced models excel in predicting agronomic traits based on genotype-phenotype relationships, outperforming traditional methods in capturing complex interactions and enhancing prediction accuracy. From random forests to convolutional neural networks, ML and DL techniques offer unprecedented capabilities in analyzing vast datasets and optimizing breeding strategies for diverse crops. Assessing the effectiveness of ML and DL models relative to traditional genomic prediction methods, such as Genomic Best Linear Unbiased Prediction, is still an area of active research. While DL exhibits promise in capturing intricate genetic interactions, traditional ML techniques and linear models continue to demonstrate efficacy, particularly with smaller datasets; the no-free-lunch theorem underscores the importance of evaluating multiple algorithms to address specific genomic prediction challenges comprehensively. In the future, the integration of AI-driven technologies, including autonomous machinery and precision irrigation systems, heralds a new era of precision agriculture. By harnessing AI and genomic advancements, farmers can enhance productivity, mitigate environmental impact, and navigate complex challenges in the quest for sustainable and high-yield agriculture. This systematic review explores current practices and research at the intersection of AI, genomics, and agriculture, illuminating the promising future of technology-driven farming paradigms.

title: Integration of Machine Learning in Plant Breeding
abstract: The integration of machine learning (ML) in plant breeding represents a groundbreaking advancement in addressing the challenges posed by climate change and diminishing genetic diversity. Climate change exacerbates agricultural challenges, particularly in semi-arid regions, where rising temperatures and extreme weather events threaten crop yields and disrupt farming stability. Traditional breeding methods, while effective, are often time-intensive and hinder the rapid development of climate-resilient crop varieties. In this context, ML techniques such as support vector regression and deep learning models can significantly enhance predictive accuracy and efficiency in phenotype prediction and genomic analysis, allowing for the identification of key traits and complex interactions between genotype and environment. This chapter explores the potential of ML to transform phenotypic selection by enabling the analysis of vast datasets to uncover intricate patterns and associations that traditional methods might overlook. By improving the precision of trait prediction, ML enhances breeding outcomes, facilitating the development of crop varieties that can withstand unpredictable climatic conditions. Moreover, ML methods are particularly adept at managing high-dimensional inputs, making them well-suited to the complexities of modern genomic data. Despite the promising applications of ML in plant breeding, several challenges remain, including the integration of multiomics data and the need for robust feature engineering. The reliance on large datasets can lead to overfitting and necessitate substantial computational resources, which may impede widespread adoption. This chapter aims to address these limitations and discuss innovative approaches that combine traditional breeding techniques with ML to optimize breeding cycles and improve decision-making processes. By harnessing the synergies between these methodologies, we can enhance the sustainability of agricultural systems and ensure food security in the face of ongoing environmental changes.

title: Genetic Gains in Crop Yield Through Genomic Selection Under Drought Stress
abstract: Drought stress remains a significant hurdle in worldwide agriculture, requiring creative methods to guarantee food security when faced with unfavorable climate conditions. This section delves into the game-changing possibilities of genomic selection (GS) for boosting crop yields under drought stress. GS represents a state-of-the-art breeding approach that utilizes advanced genomic technologies to forecast the performance of individual plants through their genetic composition. By combining genetic markers with extensive phenotypic information, breeders can opt for plants with elevated drought resilience and heightened yield capabilities. The outset of this chapter involves an exploration of the importance of drought stress within contemporary agriculture and the imperative for robust crop cultivars. The inception of the GS concept is introduced, highlighting its capacity to expedite breeding cycles, refine precision in trait prognosis, and facilitate the concurrent assimilation of numerous coveted traits. The underlying molecular mechanisms responsible for drought tolerance are scrutinized, offering valuable perspectives on plausible genetic focal points for bolstering crop durability. The chapter further delves into the pivotal significance of meticulous phenotyping and its seamless integration with cutting-edge genotyping technologies. Advanced techniques for quantifying drought-related attributes, such as stomatal conductance, root structure, and photosynthetic efficacy, are thoroughly examined. Diverse genotyping tactics, encompassing single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and next-generation sequencing, are scrutinized, along with the integration of marker-assisted selection into GS workflows. The elucidation of statistical models for genomic prediction encompasses mathematical frameworks such as ridge regression, Bayesian approaches, and machine learning algorithms. Future prospects and challenges of GS within drought-resilient crop cultivation are deliberated, encompassing strategies to surmount genetic intricacies and the latent potential of emerging technologies such as genome editing. The chapter culminates by underscoring the requisite collaborative endeavors among scientists, breeders, policymakers, and stakeholders, essential for harnessing the complete potential of GS and guaranteeing sustainable global food security amidst the evolution of climatic conditions.

title: Smart and Sustainable Agriculture
abstract: The digital farming ecosystem involves multiple stakeholders including farmers, customers, vendors, consumers, retail malls, and a third party. The system involves multiple processes including farming, the use of pesticides, food security, buying, lending, and auction. The system is highly complex in nature involving data sources in heterogeneous formats involving multiple stakeholders and processes that are crucial. In recent times, terms like smart agriculture, sustainable agriculture, and precision agriculture have started gaining momentum. The technology is the “cure” or “curse.” The cure lies in the implementation of multiple technologies such as blockchain, the Internet of Things, big data analytics, machine learning, artificial intelligence, and soft computing. Also, it may become a curse for maintaining the agricultural ecosystem related to privacy concerns, security issues, data leakage, etc. It has become very crucial to design robust technology strategies to solve agriculture problems and even to predict the problems that may arise in the future. The current agriculture system has to look beyond the horizon so that the door to new problems and solutions is opened to give a wide spectrum to the agriculture system worldwide. The chapters provide multiple dimensions of agriculture with technology at heart.

title: Integrating IoT, Sensors, and Machine Learning for Enhancing Crop Yield and Irrigation Efficiency Systems
abstract: Ensuring world food security depends on agricultural output; hence, problems such as water constraints, climatic unpredictability, and ineffective irrigation techniques compromise ideal crop production. This work proposes an integrated framework using sophisticated sensor systems, Internet of Things (IoT) technology, and machine learning models to improve irrigation efficiency and agricultural output. IoT-enabled sensors in the proposed system track important environmental factors like soil moisture, temperature, and humidity in real-time. These sensors’ data is analyzed using machine learning techniques to forecast crop water needs, therefore guaranteeing exact and flexible irrigation management. Integration of predictive analytics helps the system maximize water distribution, therefore reducing resource waste and enhancing crop health. Field tests show that this method greatly increases irrigation efficiency and raises crop production. The results show the possibilities of IoT-driven solutions in changing conventional farming methods by encouraging sustainable water use and raising general agricultural production. This study offers a scalable and efficient solution for contemporary precision farming systems, therefore expanding the already increasing corpus of knowledge on smart agriculture.

title: Smart Farming Technologies
abstract: The convergence of the Internet of Things (IoT), data analytics, and machine learning is transforming contemporary agriculture, resulting in the development of smart farming and precision agriculture. The current review synthesizes results of 24 seminal studies that discuss varied applications of IoT-based technologies across agricultural production. These reports identify improvements in sensor networks, wireless communications, cloud platforms, and data-driven decision-making software that allow for real-time monitoring, efficient irrigation, pest management, and yield forecasting. The application of big data and artificial intelligence has been invaluable in converting raw data into useful information, enhancing farm productivity, sustainability, and profitability. While the potential is clear, scalability, interoperability, data security, infrastructure capacity, and rural adoption obstacles continue to exist. Multiple studies also highlight the need for leveraging geospatial data and wireless sensor networks for improving decision-making accuracy. The combination of smart devices and analytics not only helps in solving food security problems but also supports global initiatives to implement sustainable agriculture and climate resilience. This systematic review serves as a basis for future research and deployment plans, with the aim of overcoming practical limitations and increasing technological resilience in heterogeneous agro-ecosystems.

title: Big Data and Cloud Computing for Agricultural Decision Support
abstract: The convergence of cloud computing, big data analytics, and Internet of Things (IoT) technologies is transforming farming practices with smart decision-making systems. This paper provides an exhaustive overview of recent developments in cloud-based agricultural Decision Support Systems (DSS), their functions to enhance productivity, sustainability, and operations efficiency. A scan of 25 most significant studies shows that distributed processing models, geospatial processing, machine learning, and real-time sensor data are critical to facilitating precision agriculture and data-driven decision-making. Different models—ranging from environment monitoring systems to complaint management systems—show how integrating cloud infrastructure with AI methodologies is efficient in crop care, resource allocation, and environmental monitoring. Additionally, various research presents integrated platforms assisting smallholder farmers with real-time advice, weather forecasts, and risk management. Data standardization, system integration, and security issues remain challenges, but technologies such as blockchain incorporation and smart architecture are resolving them. This article highlights the increasing importance of cloud-based smart farming and how it can help resolve the threat of global food security while ensuring sustainable agriculture.

title: Crop Product Health Management System Using DL, Precision Irrigation System Using Internet of Things and DL/ML
abstract: Effective water management and crop health greatly affect agricultural sustainability and production. This paper suggests an integrated Crop Product Health Management System using Deep Learning (DL) for disease detection and Precision Irrigation System driven by the Internet of Things (IoT) and Machine Learning (ML) to maximize water use. The technology detects illnesses, nutrient shortages, and insect infestations in real-time using com-puter vision-based DL models to examine crop photos. IoT-enabled soil moisture sensors, weather data, and predictive ML models concurrently provide exact irrigation scheduling, therefore guaranteeing appropriate water distribution depending on real-time environmental circumstances. By means of real-time insights, water waste reduction, and crop health enhancement, the suggested framework improves decision-making. While ML algorithms examine sensor data to forecast irrigation needs, the DL models are trained on vast sets of plant disease photos. Comparatively to conventional techniques, experimental findings show better yield quality, lower water usage, and efficient disease control. This study emphasizes the possibilities of artificial intelligence-driven solutions for smart agriculture so guaranteeing food security and sustainable farming methods. Modern agricultural systems can benefit from a strong, scalable solution provided by the combination of DL, IoT, and ML, hence driving farming more data-driven and resource-efficient.

title: Weather Forecasting and Crop Yield Prediction Using AI/ML Models
abstract: Agriculture is highly dependent on weather conditions, and accurate forecasting is crucial for optimizing crop yield and resource utilization. Traditional weather prediction and crop yield estimation methods often struggle with accuracy due to the complexity of climate patterns and environmental factors. This research explores the application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) models for weather forecasting and crop yield prediction to enhance agricultural decision-making. The study integrates multiple data sources, including satellite imagery, meteorological data, soil properties, and historical crop production records, to train predictive models. Various AI/ML techniques, such as deep learning, regression models, and time-series forecasting, are evaluated for their effectiveness in predicting climatic variations and crop productivity. The proposed approach aims to improve the precision of weather predictions and yield estimates, enabling farmers and policymakers to make data-driven decisions that enhance food security and sustainable farming practices. Experimental results demonstrate the potential of AI-driven models in providing accurate and real-time insights, reducing the risks associated with extreme weather events and inefficient resource allocation. This research contributes to the advancement of smart agriculture by leveraging AI and ML technologies to develop a robust and scalable framework for predictive analytics in agriculture.

title: Reviewing Advances in Image‐Based Plant Disease Detection
abstract: All economies on the earth are built on agriculture. One of the key factors affecting a nation's internal market conditions is crop production. In any nation, agricultural productivity is a crucial requirement for economic growth. Anticipated crop production is expected to vary globally due to a multitude of reasons. These include varying soil fertility levels, irregular rainfall patterns, chemical contamination of the water supply, and excessive use of fertilizers. One of the most common issues facing the world today is the significant loss of production caused by illness. The heyday of machine learning is represented by deep learning, which has progressively taken the lead as the most popular method across many industries. The various imaging technologies used in plant disease detection are next covered, with an emphasis on their benefits and drawbacks. These include visible light imaging, hyperspectral imaging, and thermal imaging. The study evaluates the promise and the challenges associated with image-based disease detection systems in real agricultural settings. Scalability, environmental variability, model generalization, and dataset availability are some of the difficulties it addresses. It also looks at potential paths for the next studies, such as the application of multimodal imaging, the creation of sturdy transfer learning frameworks, and the field implementation of low-cost, portable imaging equipment. In conclusion, this study provides a comprehensive review of the most recent advancements in image-based plant disease detection, highlighting its revolutionary potential for yield forecasting, crop health management, and ultimately global food security.

title: Leveraging ResNeXt50 and LSTM for Enhanced Plant Disease Detection
abstract: This chapter explores the implementations of deep learning algorithms along with remote sensing technologies for precise identification and categorization of plant diseases, focusing on enhancing accuracy and efficiency in agricultural practices. This research study intends to succeed in building a hybrid model for the classification and forecasting of diseased plants with high accuracy. Plant disease detection and classification is a critical field of study within agricultural science and technology. It involves identifying and categorizing diseases affecting plants to ensure timely and effective management practices. Early and accurate identification of plant diseases is crucial to minimize crop loss, maintain food security, and reduce the use of pesticides, which can have adverse environmental and health effects. In any country, both the yield and the quality of agricultural products are essential for the success of agriculture. Plant disease (i.e. abnormal growth or functionality) detection is tough work, which has prompted numerous investigators to apply image processing, machine learning (ML), computer vision, and big data analytics, etc., techniques, which make the challenging assignment easier. The proposed approach integrates the deep convolutional neural network ResNeXt50 with long short-term memory (LSTM) networks to tackle the dual tasks of plant leaf disease classification and segmentation. The ResNeXt50 backbone extracts intricate spatial features from plant leaf images, while the LSTM component models the temporal dynamics of disease progression. This hybrid model exploits the hierarchical feature representation of ResNeXt50 and the sequential learning capabilities of LSTM to enhance accuracy and contextual understanding of plant leaf diseases. The model's training accuracy was enhanced to a maximum of 99.74% and a validation accuracy of 95.44%, scoring 94% in F1, 96% in recall, and 96% in accuracy. Comparative analysis reveals that the ResNeXt50 + LSTM model outperforms other classifiers, including Inception V3, AlexNet, ResNet50, and VGG16, addressing overfitting and vanishing gradient issues. The model demonstrates superior performance in handling imbalanced data and excels in plant disease prediction, validated through various benchmarks and datasets. This study confirms the hybrid model's robustness and potential for practical application in plant pathology.

title: Harvesting Tomorrow
abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in agriculture has revolutionized the sector and given farmers access to safe, secure, practicable, and sufficiently productive farming practices for the modern day. This technological revolution has been sparked by precision agriculture, which makes use of AI and its algorithms to analyze large amounts of data based on crop conditions, soil characteristics, and climate variables. The algorithms then provide actionable insights. Drones, satellite imaging, and Internet of Things sensors allow farmers to remotely monitor their crops in real time, maximizing resource efficiency and minimizing environmental impact. Furthermore, yield prediction, disease and pest warning, and timely planting are greatly enhanced by automated processing that makes use of forecast analytics and machine learning breakthroughs. The agricultural sector might potentially increase its profitability by managing risks more effectively, making better decisions, and gaining actionable insights from big data and improved analytics. In the midst of the numerous issues affecting food security in the modern world, AI in agriculture is presented as a long-term solution. These issues include climate change, population growth, resource scarcity, and rising food production demands. However, in order to fully utilize AI to benefit humanity, we require strong cross-branch collaboration, secure legal frameworks, and appropriate allocation of computational resources. This chapter highlights not only the immense potential of AI in agriculture but also the necessity of regulatory oversight, ethical framing, and an appropriate and improved model of innovation for the revolutionary capacity of AI for the societal good. Thus, the current chapter delves deeper into AI's multidimensional and revolutionary relevance in modern agriculture and how it might overcome current obstacles while creating new chances based on the analysis of AI's real-life possibilities.

title: AI Technology for Protection of Water Supplies from Contamination to Produce Healthy Foods
abstract: Ensuring clean and safe water supplies is critical for sustainable agriculture and the production of healthy foods. AI technology plays a transformative role in monitoring and protecting water resources from contamination, thereby supporting food security and public health. By utilizing machine learning algorithms, real-time sensors, and predictive models, AI can detect and predict waterborne pollutants, optimize water usage, and provide early warning systems for contamination events. This integration of AI into water management enhances efficiency, prevents the spread of harmful contaminants, and promotes environmentally sustainable farming practices, ensuring the production of safe, healthy foods.

title: Data‐Driven Approaches for Sustainable Agriculture and Food Security
abstract: The advent of data-driven methods is successfully addressing the issues of food security and sustainable agriculture. By 2050, there will likely be 9.7 billion people on the planet, making it critical to increase agricultural output while reducing negative environmental effects. This summary offers insights into the transformative impact of data-driven approaches on the agricultural sector, contributing significantly to the attainment of sustainable agriculture and food security objectives. A crucial element of data-driven methodologies involves gathering and analyzing extensive agricultural data. High-resolution data covering a range of agricultural topics, such as soil conditions, weather patterns, crop growth, and insect infestations, has been made easier by developments in sensor technology, satellite photography, and remote sensing. These data sources enable farmers and policy-makers to make informed choices about crop selection, pest management tactics, and resource allocation when combined with machine learning algorithms and data analytics. Precision agriculture, which applies site-specific interventions to maximize crop yields while limiting resource inputs like water, fertilizer, and pesticides, is also made possible by data-driven methodologies. Farmers can adjust their methods to meet the particular needs of each field by analyzing data on crop health, nutrient levels, and soil moisture. By reducing water and chemical waste, this focused strategy not only increases output but also lessens the environmental effect of agriculture. In addition to optimizing resource allocation, data-driven approaches contribute to enhancing resilience in agriculture. Given the significant challenges posed by climate change to food security, including the heightened frequency and severity of extreme weather events, analyzing historical climate data and utilizing predictive models allow farmers to anticipate weather patterns. This proactive approach enables them to adjust planting and harvesting schedules accordingly, minimizing crop losses and ensuring a stable food supply.

title: Sustainable Development in Agriculture
abstract: Developing sustainable techniques for agriculture and soil management is essential for ensuring food security, protecting natural resources, and promoting sustainable livelihoods and exploring the importance of research and exploration in this field, highlighting key research questions related to soil health, water management, agricultural technologies, policy interventions, and the impacts of climate change. It emphasizes the need for interdisciplinary approaches that integrate social, economic, and environmental considerations to promote sustainable techniques for agriculture and soil management. This involves investigating the impacts of different agricultural practices on the environment and human health and exploring innovative approaches to improving agricultural productivity while minimizing negative effects on natural resources. This will involve exploring the potential for small-scale and diversified farming systems like India to support sustainable livelihoods or assessing the effectiveness of different policy interventions by the government. It will involve field research to understand the soil quality, climate, and other factors that affect crop production and explore the potential for new approaches to farming, such as agro forestry, to improve soil health, reduce erosion, and enhance biodiversity. Based on the field research and data, an analysis will be carried out and a machine learning model will predict the crops, and manures to be added to improve soil fertility without harming the natural resources climatic conditions, and their impact during every phase. Our research may also be used to develop a country-while centralized system that will help the farmers and the government to grow the demanded crops and this will also reduce the wastage of grains in cases of overproduction. It will also uplift the farmers by providing them with an adequate sum of money for their products since they will be growing the demanded crops only. Overall, sustainable techniques for agriculture and soil management are essential for ensuring that agricultural production can meet the needs of a growing global population while protecting natural resources and supporting sustainable livelihoods.

title: Agriculture Meets Blockchain for Crop Monitoring and Prediction Using Machine Learning Techniques
abstract: Early prediction of crops plays an important role in ensuring food stability. Given the escalating global demand for food production and the complexities presented by climate change, there is an escalating demand for precise and effective techniques to forecast and oversee crop growth. Leveraging historical data encompassing variables such as climate conditions, soil attributes, crop varieties, and agricultural practices, Machine Learning (ML) models are employed to identify the most suitable crop for cultivation. The paper begins by discussing the importance of accurate crop forecasting and monitoring for sustainable agriculture and food security. In addition to addressing the challenges related to data collection, preprocessing, and model training in the context of crop prediction, this paper systematically surveys the state-of-the-art ML models used in various stages of the crop life cycle, from pre-planting decision-making to post-harvest analysis. Various types of data sources including weather data, soil conditions, and historical yield records, are explored as inputs for ML algorithm. This work presents a comprehensive approach that uses Machine Learning (ML) algorithms to improve crop selection and determine the ideal time to apply pesticides. In addition to crop selection, ML algorithms are to determine optimal timing for pesticide application. This integrated approach not only enhances agricultural productivity and profitability but also promotes environmental sustainability by optimizing pesticide application and minimizing adverse effects on ecosystems. Through the integration of machine learning methods with precision agricultural principles, this work advances the use of data to inform decisions in modern farming practices. It encourages environmentally conscious crop management practices that balance economic feasibility with sustainability.

title: Farming 4.0
abstract: Agriculture is one of the major sectors that have been considered to be essential to ensuring food security. The world's population is growing, and there are many natural factors that make nourishing billions of people challenging. The application of Internet of Things (IoT) in agriculture is revolutionizing the field and creating opportunities for accurate monitoring and data-driven farming. The Internet of Things with the sensors and unmanned aircraft, which helps in tracking the farming lands based on the phenomenon of humidity, crop performance, livestock, and temperature are termed as Farming 4.0. This research chapter holds the smart agriculture concept that highlights the usage of Internet of Things in its evolutionary concept. This nominally increases the food output, as the year 2050 is predicted to have food shortage due to growing population, traditional farming methods, and outdated skills of farmers in field pattern. This fine goal has led to the enlarged connectivity between the digital scale of the marketed items using the internet. The loss reduction with increase in yield values is determined by the process of gathering data continuously with a precise level of monitoring. By considering the periodic data with the current trends, the farmers predict the yield with the disease outbreaks enhancing the consumer preferences with accurate data-driven methods. Making decisions based on strategic values helps in choosing the best strategic plan. Managing the strategies in remote locations using the IoT helps in providing the data with real-time access creating web alerts responding to disease outbreak with a high range of accuracy at nominal consumer preferences. This is made possible by connecting the sensors to the land. This helps in monitoring the storage conditions optimizing the tracking of shipments on agricultural supply chain values. This ensures producing high- quality food with waste reduction enhancing the efficiency of the supply chain process. The data gathered using the IoT based on artificial intelligence and various training procedures help the supporting system with decisions packed, thus highlighting suggestions and various insights. The agro-based sensor devices used for evaluation are connected to farming, service types, and the readiness of actual technological levels chosen for practicing. The results are framed with the process of investigating the technologies at the digital level such as machine learning embedded on the robotic systems and the Internet of Things. Thus, embracing security with IoT protocols helps to protect the assets on the farmland fostering long-term technological viability. Thus, the future of agriculture lies in leveraging the global IoT, which helps in achieving improved choices and accurate level of monitoring with suitable practices.

title: Nutrition in Emergencies
abstract: The global problem of hunger is most acutely seen in regions facing emergencies, including climate change, armed conflicts and natural disasters. Economic and political issues are drivers of hunger in emergency situations. Fluctuations in food prices and wages and major changes to government policies can result in significant disruptions to food security. Natural disasters and climate change result in food shortages. The impact of climate change, including melting glaciers as well as periods of more severe flooding and droughts in many regions of the world, is expected to affect the quality and quantity of available water for human populations. Armed conflict results in malnutrition among populations. Early warning signs of humanitarian crises may be seen by monitoring accelerating factors and decelerating factors associated with crises. Preventative strategies such as micronutrient fortification and investments in education and agriculture can help to prevent or lessen the severity of emergencies.

title: Machine Learning for Modeling Plant Abiotic Stress Responses
abstract: Machine learning (ML) offers a transformative approach to modeling plant abiotic stress responses, including drought, salinity, extreme temperatures, and nutrient deficiencies, which are significant threats to agricultural productivity. Because plant systems are complicated, traditional approaches rely on physiological and genetic tests, which may be sluggish. ML, on the other hand, can examine enormous datasets to find trends and forecast plant responses to stress, which aids in the development of robust crops. For example, by combining information from genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic sources, ML may predict plant phenotypes and help identify features that are resistant to stress. Additionally, machine learning models gene regulatory networks by predicting the relationships that govern stress responses using supervised learning techniques like random forests. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) offer high-throughput picture processing, further permitting real-time monitoring of plant health under stress by identifying signs such as chlorosis or wilting. Furthermore, by integrating multi-omics data, ML enables deep learning models to uncover intricate connections between genes, proteins, and metabolites that could otherwise be missed. With the ability to simulate different stress conditions, predictive models for stress response prediction using machine learning show significant potential for precision agriculture. This can assist in optimizing crop management and breeding efforts. Supervised learning to predict phenotypes, unsupervised clustering to find new stress-responsive genes, and deep learning to manage massive datasets for high-throughput phenotyping are common approaches. There are still issues, though, including the accessibility of high-quality information, the capacity of models to generalize across different species, and the interpretability of intricate models. Resolving these problems is essential to the full potential of ML in plant research. As machine learning continues to progress, it has the potential to significantly improve our capacity to develop crops that are resistant to environmental stressors and climate change, paving the way for more sustainable agriculture and increased food security. Abiotic stressors that adversely affect plant development and agricultural output include salt, drought, high temperatures, and nutritional deficits. Developing crops that are robust to stress requires an understanding of and ability to predict plant responses to various pressures. Because of the complexity of plant systems, traditional approaches for researching abiotic stress responses frequently rely on physiological and genetic tests, which can be time-consuming. To mimic these answers, ML provides a potent substitute by examining large datasets to spot trends, forecast results, and even offer creative solutions.

title: Machine Learning‐Driven Smart Agriculture
abstract: Innovation in smart agriculture is being made possible by the emergence of machine learning (ML), which is making the agricultural sector more productive and sustainable. This study explores the various uses of ML in agriculture, highlighting how precision farming may maximize yield, improve resource management, and boost crop resilience. Predictive analytics for disease and pest outbreaks, which enable prompt interventions and reduce crop losses, is one of the study's key uses. In order to guarantee efficient water use while preserving resources, automated irrigation systems also use ML to assess soil moisture content and weather predictions. To assist with supply chain management and market planning, crop yield prediction models project production levels based on past data and present circumstances. There are obstacles to overcome before applying ML to agricultural practices that can fully reap the potential benefits. Widespread adoption of technology will require addressing issues including data quality, platform integration, and technology accessibility for smallholder farmers. Moreover, educational programs that equip farmers with the know-how to use ML tools efficiently are desperately needed. This study emphasizes how important ML is to solving today's complicated agricultural problems, such as climate change and food security. The agriculture industry may take a step toward a more robust and sustainable future by implementing ML-driven techniques, especially precision farming. Finally, this study demonstrates how ML can alter conventional farming practices and build an agricultural ecosystem that is more productive, highlighting the technology's transformative potential.

title: The Future Farming: Machine Learning and Crop Health
abstract: In traditional crop management, the selection of crops, seeds, varieties, seasonal cropping, farming practices, postharvest strategies, and marketing also face multi-dimensional issues or drawbacks from the availability of resources, and the lack of knowledge in novel farming and marketing trends resulting in failure and changes to sustainable agriculture is questioned one. In these circumstances, the swift progress of technology, coupled with the urgent issues surrounding global food security, has established machine learning (ML) as a pivotal element in agriculture, especially in the management of crop health. On the other side, growth rate of the population increased rapidly with unpredictable, demand for food production, respectively. This abstract examines the emerging concept of “future farming,” wherein ML algorithms possess the capability to analyze extensive datasets from diverse sources, such as satellite imagery, soil sensors, and climate information. These algorithms also facilitate predictive modeling to anticipate potential threats to crop health, including pests, diseases, and environmental stressors. By incorporating these advanced technologies, farmers can implement precision agriculture techniques that enable customized interventions, thereby reducing waste and environmental impact while enhancing productivity. The provision of real-time data and insights promotes data-driven decision-making, allowing farmers to take proactive measures instead of merely responding to issues as they arise. Additionally, advancements in explainable AI are improving the clarity of ML models, fostering trust, and encouraging the adoption of these innovations among agricultural stakeholders. Nonetheless, the effective integration of ML in agriculture encounters considerable obstacles, such as data quality concerns, the intricacies of biological systems, and the need for interdisciplinary collaboration among agronomists, data scientists, and farmers. Overcoming these challenges is essential to fully realize the potential of ML in advancing sustainable agricultural practices. Looking forward, the collaboration between ML and innovative crop management strategies holds the promise of a future in farming that is not only more efficient and resilient but also aligned with ecological sustainability and food security, thus ushering in a new era of agricultural productivity in response to global challenges.

title: Federated Learning–Based Approach for Crop Recommendation and Market Stability in Agriculture
abstract: The agricultural sector, particularly in India, faces significant challenges such as crop overproduction, price volatility, and post-harvest losses, which lead to substantial financial losses for farmers and instability in food markets. To address these challenges, this research introduces a federated learning–based system designed to optimize crop production and enhance market stability by offering personalized, data-driven recommendations while maintaining farmer data privacy. Unlike traditional machine learning models that centralize data, federated learning allows for decentralized data processing where models are trained locally on farmer devices, and only model parameters are shared, preserving the confidentiality of sensitive agricultural data. This dual-layer approach incorporates a variety of data sources including Internet-of-Things sensors, market trends, weather conditions, and farmer inputs, enabling the system to deliver tailored crop recommendations that consider regional conditions, resource availability, and market demand. The proposed system enhances decision-making for both small and large-scale farmers by offering dynamic and real-time crop suggestions that help prevent overproduction and align with current market needs. It integrates feedback from farmers after each harvest, continually refining the model to improve accuracy and relevance. The system also takes into account infrastructure capabilities such as storage and transportation, offering crop recommendations that reduce spoilage and optimize profitability. By analyzing real-time market trends and incorporating price prediction algorithms, the system helps farmers navigate fluctuating prices and avoid market saturation. This research highlights the potential of federated learning in promoting equitable market participation, reducing food wastage, and ensuring a more stable and sustainable agricultural sector. This study's federated learning approach not only preserves privacy and minimizes communication costs but also ensures the scalability of the system across diverse farming regions. Future developments of this system may include the integration of blockchain for enhanced data security and transparency, as well as the incorporation of government policies and support systems to further drive sustainable agricultural practices. The system offers a promising solution to the persistent challenges in agriculture, enabling farmers to make informed, data-driven decisions while maintaining control over their sensitive data.

title: Machine Learning for Precision Epigenetic Modification in Plants
abstract: The accelerating global population and climate instability demand innovative, data-driven breeding strategies to ensure food security. Epigenetic mechanisms, such as DNA methylation, histone modifications, chromatin remodeling, and RNA-mediated regulation, govern plant development, stress adaptation, and transgenerational resilience. These reversible and heritable marks dynamically modulate chromatin accessibility and gene expression, providing a flexible interface between genotype and environment. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have transformed plant epigenetics by enabling the precise prediction, interpretation, and manipulation of regulatory marks. Deep learning (DL) architectures that integrate genomic, transcriptomic, and epigenomic data can now decode the multilayered interactions governing gene regulation. ML algorithms, such as random forests (RFs), extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), and support vector machines (SVMs), together with DL frameworks including neural networks, generative models, and reinforcement learning systems, have achieved high accuracy in predicting methylation and histone modification dynamics while advancing rational epigenome design. AI-guided clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/dCas-based epigenetic genome editing (epi-GED) platforms further provide nonmutagenic and reversible control of gene expression through targeted modification of methylation or histone marks. By coupling computational prediction with molecular precision, ML-driven epigenetic engineering bridges in silico inference with in planta application, advancing intelligent design breeding. The convergence of AI, multiomics integration, and epigenetic modulation heralds a paradigm shift toward sustainable, adaptive, and high-yield crop development for resilient agriculture in a changing climate.

title: Machine Learning Models for Crop Disease Detection
abstract: Crop disease detection is being revolutionized by machine learning algorithms, which provide creative and effective answers to age-old agricultural problems. This chapter explores the use of several machine learning methods for crop disease identification and diagnosis, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Support Vector Machines (SVMs), Random Forests, and Transfer Learning. These models can identify diseases early, reducing yield losses and improving food security by utilizing big datasets that include photos and environmental factors. By combining machine learning, IoT technologies, and predictive analytics, farmers can better track crop health in real time and take preventative measures. This chapter focuses on the effectiveness of machine learning techniques in agriculture, as well as their potential to revolutionize crop management, increase sustainability, and ensure a steady supply of food to the world's rising population. Machine learning is projected to have a greater impact on how agriculture evolves in the future as technology advances.

title: IoT‐Based Soil Nutrition Water Management and Detection of Plant Diseases for Smart Agriculture
abstract: In the coming years, as relocation is happening towards Industrialization 5.0, farmers will be provided with upgraded technologies that integrate artificial intelligence. These developing technologies will take advantage of blockchain for security reasons owing to cyber warfare. Farmers experience multiple challenges in terms of food security and dependence on imported goods. The proper utilization of modern technologies that involve deep learning algorithms and IoT sensors for soil testing will undoubtedly solve farmers’ difficulties. The Proposed model is a framework for IoT soil nutrition that utilizes a machine-learning model to optimize data collected from temperature and humidity sensors. This model not only predicts the crop that will be suitable based on soil testing, but also considers soil nutrition testing. The subsequent section analyses crop disease prediction applying the Rexnet 150 deep learning algorithm, which has recently been shown to33 have the highest degree of accuracy exhibited by any deep learning system. This approach additionally incorporates water automation in farmers’ agriculture fields, where the entire system is implemented to eliminate superfluous water from their crops, thereby enhancing crop yield. The entire procedure collaborates with Flask generating a web app interface for users, who should be a native speakers so that farmers can access and comprehend the format.

title: Zwitterionic Materials for Water Treatment and Food Packaging: Synthesis, Performance, and Machine Learning‐Driven Design
abstract: The growing demand for high‐performance materials in water treatment and food packaging has intensified research into zwitterionic‐based structures due to their exceptional hydrophilicity, fouling resistance, and functional versatility. This review presents a comprehensive analysis of recent advances in the synthesis, characterization, and performance evaluation of zwitterionic materials for these critical applications, with particular emphasis on emerging machine learning approaches that enable their rational design and optimization. By summarizing key findings and identifying current challenges, this work aims to bridge the gap between laboratory‐scale innovations and real‐world implementation. Among various synthesis strategies, polymerization has emerged as the most effective method for incorporating zwitterionic functionalities. Morphological studies further demonstrate that zwitterionic modification significantly enhances both adsorptive and barrier properties. Machine learning models have shown strong potential in accelerating the development of zwitterionic materials by establishing structure–property relationships that predict and optimize antifouling performance. By integrating insights from multiple disciplines, this review outlines a strategic framework for transforming fundamental research into practical solutions that promote environmental sustainability and food security.

title: Machine learning for food security: Principles for transparency and usability
abstract: Abstract Machine learning (ML) holds potential to predict hunger crises before they occur. Yet, ML models embed crucial choices that affect their utility. We develop a prototype model to predict food insecurity across three countries in sub‐Saharan Africa. Readily available data on prices, assets, and weather all influence our model predictions. Our model obtains 55%–84% accuracy, substantially outperforming both a logit and ML models using only time and location. We highlight key principles for transparency and demonstrate how modeling choices between recall and accuracy can be tailored to policy‐maker needs. Our work provides a path for future modeling efforts in this area.

title: A machine learning‐based exploration of resilience and food security
abstract: Abstract Leveraging advancements in remote data collection and using the Food Insecurity Experience Scale (FIES) as a proxy measure of resilience, we show that machine learning models (such as Gradient Boosting Classifier, eXtreme Gradient Boosting, and Artificial Neural Networks), can predict resilience with relatively high accuracy (up to 81%). Key household‐level predictors include access to financial institutions, asset ownership, the adoption of agricultural mechanization as evidenced by the use of tractors, the number of crops cultivated, and ownership of nonfarm enterprises. Our analysis offers insights to researchers and policymakers interested in the development of targeted interventions to bolster household resilience.

title: Understanding Egg Price Volatility and Policy Implications in the U.S. With Machine Learning
abstract: ABSTRACT Eggs are an inexpensive and sustainable source of proteins, but volatility in the U.S. egg prices has intensified in recent years, raising concerns over food affordability and market stability. This study examines the drivers of U.S. egg price dynamics over 2004–2025 using a two‐stage framework that combines LASSO‐based variable selection with an ARIMAX forecasting model. The results reveal strong price persistence, together with significant impacts of energy, feed costs and seasonal demand. The influence of avian influenza is strongly time‐dependent, with limited effects in full‐sample averages but significant impacts during high‐intensity outbreak periods, particularly in the mid‐2010s and after 2022. Out‐of‐sample forecasts indicate that the LASSO‐ARIMAX model reduces forecast errors by more than 60% relative to a univariate ARIMA benchmark. These findings suggest that stabilizing key input costs, strengthening timely epidemiological surveillance, and proactively managing predictable seasonal demand pressures are more effective than relying on any single explanatory factor.

title: Behavioral Coping With Food Price Inflation: Patterns Among U.S. Households
abstract: ABSTRACT Recent food price inflation has placed substantial pressure on household budgets, food security, and mental well‐being. Using Household Pulse Survey data, we combine k‐modes clustering and Double Machine Learning to identify distinct household coping groups and examine differences in how households respond to rising food prices across groups. Results show that higher food prices are associated with increased grocery and prepared meal spending, elevate risks of food insufficiency, and worsen mental health conditions, with heterogeneity across coping groups. Households employing moderate substitution strategies show limited buffering, while those using more intensive coping behaviors remain highly vulnerable, highlighting the need for policy responses that address the multiple, co‐occurring dimensions of hardship including food access, financial strain, and mental health, rather than any single dimension in isolation.

title: Local fishers’ knowledge on the ecology, economic importance, and threats faced by populations of African snakehead fish, Parachanna obscura , within Côte d'Ivoire freshwater ecosystems
abstract: Abstract Traditionally, population sizes, ecology, and threats to species and their habitats have been obtained by empirical scientific studies. However, the knowledge of local and indigenous communities worldwide has been acknowledged as an extremely rich and underused source of information on how the environment, biodiversity, and local conditions are changing over time. In this view, the objective of the study was to investigate local fishers’ knowledge of local names, habitats, uses, market price, change in population abundance, and threats faced by the snakehead fish ( Parachanna obscura ) in Ivorian freshwaters. The study was conducted using face‐to‐face interviews and a structured questionnaire with 381 fishers during the period from October 2020 to February 2021. The results show that this fish species is strongly appreciated for the good taste of its flesh, with market prices varying between 1.5 and 3€ on average. All respondents confirmed that the species is not yet produced in aquaculture and mentioned their willingness to support its introduction into aquaculture. Several local names of P. obscura fish were recorded, with ‘Sounôgô‐djêguê’ (used in 36% of fishers’ ethnic groups), ‘Pino’ (21%), and ‘Édjoué‐bile’ (21%) being the most popular names used in Ivorian fishers’ communities. All respondents agreed that P. obscura is a potamodromous fish species living preferably in wetlands, rivers, lakes, and streams. A significant decrease in the abundance of this fish was observed by 71% of fishers, perceived mainly due to overfishing, deforestation around watersheds, habitat destruction/modification, obnoxious fishing practices, pesticide use in farms close to watersheds, and climate change, especially lack of rainfall. The study clearly demonstrated the importance of local ecological knowledge of fishers in identifying threats to fish populations, habitat types used by the species, and other relevant information; therefore, this ecological knowledge has to be integrated into biomonitoring and conservation policy of aquatic biodiversity. The information obtained from this study is also helpful for future studies on the management and cultivation of this species.

title: Artificial intelligence in soil salinity monitoring and management: Current practices and future directions
abstract: Abstract Soil salinity remains a major threat to sustainable agriculture and global food security. Traditional management practices, including soil amendments, optimized irrigation, drainage improvement, and salt‐tolerant crops, can be effective but require precise implementation. In contrast, artificial intelligence (AI) provides advanced solutions by integrating machine learning, deep learning, predictive modeling, and Internet of Things technologies for real‐time salinity monitoring and management. This review examines current AI applications in salinity management, including salinity mapping, smart irrigation, and genetic breeding. Key results from the analyzed case studies demonstrate that AI‐driven models, such as random forest and deep convolutional neural networks, can achieve high predictive accuracy for soil electrical conductivity, with determination coefficients ( R 2 ) as high as 0.89–0.93. Furthermore, AI‐integrated irrigation systems can reduce water use by up to 30% while increasing crop yields. Additionally, coupling AI with complementary technologies like remote sensing, satellite imagery, spectral and vegetational indices, multi‐sensor data fusion, and geographic information systems allows for large‐scale, accurate assessment and prediction. Nonetheless, limitations such as data quality, technical‐know‐how, ethical concerns, sensor accuracy, and low to zero detection of specific salts are some of the challenges hindering progress in the adoption of AI. Future research must prioritize the integration of AI with indigenous knowledge systems and the creation of ethical frameworks to address socioeconomic disparities and ensure equitable access to these technologies. A hybrid approach that combines AI‐driven innovations with traditional management practices offers a promising pathway to improved soil health, agricultural sustainability, and global food security.

title: P‐WEV: PSO Based Weighted Ensemble Technique for Agricultural Food Price Volatility Modeling
abstract: ABSTRACT Price volatility in agricultural commodities adds uncertainty for farmers, traders, and other stakeholders in the agricultural supply chain. Sudden price changes can disrupt income predictions, making it difficult to plan and access financing. This affects not only the farming community but also rural economies and livelihood of people involved in agriculture. The present study focused on important aspect of agricultural economic stability, that is, modeling and prediction of food price volatility. Volatility models, namely, the Generalized autoregressive conditional heteroscedastic (GARCH) model, Glosten, Jagannatan, Runkle‐GARCH (GJR‐GARCH) model, exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) model and multiplicative error model (MEM), have been explored. In recent time, as the data becomes more complex and varied, it is difficult to fully understand price fluctuations with just one model. To tackle this, a novel approach called the Particle swarm optimization‐based weighted ensemble volatility model (P‐WEV) has been developed by combining predictions from four different models. To investigate the supremacy of the proposed model, data from 19 agricultural commodities, including cereals, pulses, oilseeds, vegetables, and spices, from various markets of India have been used. Interestingly, it has been found that the proposed model outperformed the other benchmark models. Moreover, an R package “PWEV” has also been developed for the implementation of the proposed model.

title: Do More Open Economies Export Less Diversely in Brazilian Agribusiness?
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper asks whether municipalities with a larger export‐to‐revenue ratio display a more concentrated bundle of exported goods in Brazilian agribusiness. Recent advances in export imputation for Brazilian municipalities allow for an analysis of the concentration profile of each municipality and its association with export openness. We make three contributions: we develop an Export‐Intensive Gini Index based on Monte Carlo simulations that isolates commodity‐specific concentration while accounting for the composition of the remaining export portfolio; we apply a double machine learning estimator to characterize the partial association between openness and concentration while controlling for hundreds of municipal characteristics covering geography, infrastructure, demography, and institutions; we provide a cross‐sectional description, for 2023, of subnational export concentration in a developing economy using production‐based rather than customs‐based trade data. Results show heterogeneity across commodities. Coffee displays the strongest positive association between export openness and concentration, followed by corn, soybeans, and sugar, while beef displays a negative coefficient. For policymakers, coffee‐ and corn‐producing municipalities face rising exposure to price volatility as global integration deepens, requiring targeted risk mitigation. Conversely, the weak relationships for soybeans and sugar suggest these sectors may offer more stable foundations for export‐oriented development.

title: Automated Discovery of Multicellular Behavior for Optimized Plant Growth and Climate Resilience
abstract: Developing resilience against climate change and establishing food security will require significant research into the responses of multicellular organisms to their environment. New approaches, such as lab automation, can substantially increase the rate of data collection for organism‐level behavior. This report describes an automated robotic system for studying multicellular organisms to accelerate scientific experimentation. The robot can simultaneously image and deliver chemicals to each organism during multiday experiments, and uses a deep learning model to automatically obtain phenotypic data. This system's abilities are demonstrated by creating a plant growth strategy for food security applications that increases biomass while decreasing nutrient utilization. Furthermore, plant growth is characterized under high salt concentrations to better understand the effects of climate change on freshwater ecosystems. This robotic approach improves lab automation for studying multicellular organisms by increasing experimental throughput, and will enable researchers to improve crop yields under uncertain climates and predict the response of organisms in changing environments.

title: Lost in aggregation? On the importance of local food price data for food poverty estimates
abstract: Abstract This paper explores within‐country variations in food price dynamics and food poverty estimates by employing local market price data and national consumer price index (CPI) data. Our results show that national CPI data may be useful for approximating national trends but they fail to detect and identify spatial variations in local trends, which have relevant welfare implications. Indeed, sourcing cereal prices from local markets, instead of national CPI statistics, leads to classification divergences in 9% of food poverty predictions, with a substantial variation in estimation errors across countries. Our findings thus underscore the need for the systematic collection of local price data to ensure effective policymaking, such as adjusting social transfers to better reflect local differences and optimizing the allocation of social funds.

title: Editorial: The Nonsense of Biofuels
abstract: Fossil fuels, like mineral oil, coal, and natural gas, are derived from the biomass of ancient times. As such, they are indirect products of photosynthesis. 1 It is therefore appropriate to ask whether we can use currently available biomass and convert it into biofuels like biodiesel and biogas. Biohydrogen might be another option. Often one can read that biofuels are CO2-neutral and therefore a weapon against global warming. Their production is also supposed to reduce the amount of petrol and natural gas to be imported into many countries, thus making them less dependent on energy import. In the following, I shall discuss the efficiencies of the processes required to produce biofuels, compare them with alternatives, draw the obvious conclusions, and present some visions. First it is necessary to discuss the efficiency of photosynthesis and to present some ideas on how to improve photosynthesis and therefore enhance biomass production. Photosynthesis comprises so-called light reactions and dark reactions. In the light reactions, the light is absorbed by the photosynthetic pigments and the energy is transferred to the reaction centers where the primary charge separation and a transmembrane transport of electrons takes place. Subsequent electron- and proton-transfer reactions lead to the synthesis of the universal biological energy carrier ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate, and NADP+ is reduced to NADPH. In the following dark reactions, NADPH and ATP are used to take carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and use it for the synthesis of carbohydrates. The photosynthetic pigments of plants can only absorb and use 47 % (related to energy) of the light of the sun ("photosynthetic active radiation"). Green light, UV, and IR irradiation are not used. In theory, 8 photons are required to reduce 2 molecules of NADP+ to NADPH, in reality, 9.4 photons are found to be necessary for this purpose. Knowing the average energy of the photons and the energy stored in the form of NADPH, it is easy to calculate that only 11.8 % of the energy of sunlight is stored in the form of NADPH. This value then also will be close to the upper limit for the efficiency of the photosynthetic production of biohydrogen. Photosynthesis is most efficient at low light intensities. It is already saturated at 20 % of full sunlight and 80 % of the light is not used. The limitations are most likely caused by the electron flow through the photosynthetic reaction centers. In addition, high light intensities lead to photodamage of a central protein subunit of the photosynthetic apparatus: plants repair their photosystem II reaction center by exchanging the D1 protein three times per hour. 3.5 billion years of evolution have not been long enough to develop a mechanism for preventing the photodamage. The dark reactions are limited by an insufficient discrimination between CO2 and O2 by the enzyme RuBisCO, which inserts CO2 into ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate. One third of the energy of the absorbed photons is believed to be required to remove the product of the O2 insertion, 2-phosphoglycolate. The second limitation is caused by the fact that photosynthesis depends on the availability of sufficient amounts of water, a condition that is not met during much of the day. As a result of the limitations described above, 4.5 % is considered as the upper limit of the photosynthetic efficiency of C3 plants. However, in reality, values of only around 1 % are observed, even for rapidly growing trees like poplars. When the yields of biofuels per hectare are known, one can easily calculate how much of the energy of the sunlight is stored in the biofuels. For German "biodiesel" which is based on rapeseed, it is less than 0.1 %, for bioethanol less than 0.2 %, and for biogas around 0.3 %. However, these values even do not take into account that more than 50 % of the energy stored in the biofuel had to be invested in order to obtain the biomass (for producing fertilizers and pesticides, for ploughing the fields, for transport) and the chemical conversion into the respective biofuel. This energy normally is derived from fossil fuels. The production and use of biofuels therefore is not CO2-neutral. In particular, the energy input is very large for the production of bioethanol from wheat or maize, and some scientists doubt that there is a net gain of energy. Certainly the reduction of CO2 release is marginal. The yield of second-generation biofuels where entire plants are used may be doubled. However, the energy input probably also increases. For example, in the production of biodiesel by the Fischer–Tropsch process, hydrogen has to be added because syngas obtained from biomass contains insufficient amounts of hydrogen. Taken together, the production of biofuels constitutes an extremely inefficient land use. This statement is true also for the production of bioethanol from sugar cane in Brazil. Commercially available photovoltaic cells already possess a conversion efficiency for sunlight of more than 15 %, the electric energy produced can be stored in electric batteries without major losses. This is about 150 times better than the storage of the energy from sunlight in biofuels. In addition, 80 % of the energy stored in the battery is used for the propulsion of a car by an electric engine, whereas a combustion engine uses only around 20 % of the energy of the gasoline for driving the wheels. Both facts together lead to the conclusion that the combination photovoltaic cells/electric battery/electric engine uses the available land 600 times better than the combination biomass/biofuels/combustion engine. It is obvious that there is some room to improve the primary steps of photosynthesis and of biomass production. First, it might be possible to increase the spectral range of the absorbable light by modifying the pigments of the light-harvesting complexes. Having pigments absorbing UV light and green light could contribute, although the prospect of having black leaves is not attractive. More realistically, one should try to change the relation of light-harvesting pigments to reaction centers by reducing the number of light-harvesting complexes funneling energy to one reaction center. This manipulation would reduce the electron flow through the reaction centers and reduce photodamage and the saturation at high light intensities. Engineering RuBisCO to increase its ability to discriminate between CO2 and O2 is still a valuable aim, in particular in the light of the discovery that the RuBisCO of red algae is much better than the plant RuBisCO in this respect. Biohydrogen production, currently employing hydrogenases connected to the reducing side of photosystem I, will only be able to compete with photovoltaic cells followed by water electrolysis if the water-splitting photosystem II can be engineered to produce hydrogen directly, either by itself or through an intermediate electron acceptor with a suited redox potential. Hydrogen production by photosystem II would reduce the number of photons required by more than 50 %. However, this protein engineering task appears to be insurmountable at present. Microalgae have been advertised as the ideal candidates for biofuel production. There are many unsupported claims about their efficiency, some even exceeding the theoretical limits of photosynthetic efficiency. I concede that microalgae could be better than land plants because of the absence of nonphotosynthetic cells and the continuous availability of water.
