title: Climate, conflicts, and variations in prices on pre‐colonial W est A frican markets for staple crops
abstract: Very little is known about the dynamics of pre‐colonial markets in Africa. This article presents a new set of data series on the pre‐colonial price of staple crops on the Gold Coast. Six hypotheses for the behaviour of market prices, found in the previous literature, are tested in this article. The results show conclusively that market prices did respond to shifts in demand and supply, for example, from climate‐induced scarcity, or to external shocks such as war. It is argued that the markets studied seem to have functioned remarkably well, given the socio‐economic and political context in which they were operating.

title: OUTLOOK 2015 – a One‐day conference, jointly hosted by the BPEX , DairyCo and EBLEX divisions of the UK 's Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board ( AHDB ), held at One, Great George Street. Westminster, London, February 2015
abstract: The 2015 conference programme explored factors that impacted on delegates' businesses in their respective sectors, including trade developments and emerging opportunities. Topics included developments and forecasting of consumer trends plus the potential for exports to the Far East. Separate breakout sessions were held for all the livestock sectors each giving an overview of the market outlook specific to that sector. This report by John Sumner, a member of the Publications Committee of the Society of Dairy Technology, focuses on the outlook for the dairy sector. Future Consumer Trends by Richard Nicholls, Head of Intelligence and Economics, The Future Foundation The presentation demonstrated that consumer trends are driven by a number of factors: economic and structural change, global views, health issues, food and new technology and consumer preferences. Careful domestic budgeting, cheap food treats, discounting and a war on waste were collectively influencing UK consumers. The view was expressed that, despite recent falls, food prices will still be higher than 8–10 years ago. Moderate growth in home food spending can be expected in the next few years although the increase in cheap treats will be relevant for the meat and milk sectors. However, the culture of budgeting and focus on price was forecast to remain. Emerging markets were expected to grow fastest over the next 5 years despite the recent slowdown, whilst globally the growing emphasis would be on eating good quality food, provenance and authenticity. From a health perspective, it was stressed that there were health trend implications for meat and dairy, which would have to be managed, and that more regulatory initiatives and demands for clear labelling should be expected. It was explained that in the coming years, mobile technology will impact on the food shopping process, the use of beacon technology will emerge providing shoppers with instant and detailed information about products (health data, calorie intake provenance and so on), all of which have implications for dairy and meat. The presentation forecast that ethical concerns will influence consumers more than at present, but not too much at the expense of price. Transparency will be vital and consumers will have a desire for new food innovations and tastes. Understanding Asia's rapidly evolving retail markets by Nick Miles, Institute of Grocery Development This presentation by IGD's Asia-Pacific Region Manager considered Asia's evolving grocery markets and the trend in grocery retailing. The population of this area is forecast to be almost 60 per cent of world population, including over one half of the world's middle classes, which will create increased demand on food supplies. The growth in the new middle class was driving up the demand for more and better products and manufactures and retailers had responded with new and exciting products. Fierce competition had resulted as retailers wanted to differentiate their products with, for example, emphasis on provenance and animal welfare. In attracting customers, retailers were capitalising on changing lifestyles, using imagery around their stores to show product quality, whilst online and digital was becoming more important. Detailed information was provided showing how Asia's grocery markets were continuing to grow with China and India being the dominant forces. Traditional trade was expected to play a strong future role, whilst consumption trends would be influenced by dense urban populations and wealth disparity. Quality and freshness and personal service would also have a large influence on trends, as would government policy. However, it was pointed out and demonstrated by market share data that modern trade was dominated by a small number of strong national retailers, but the market generally was fragmented. Data were also provided on market shares of the top 20 grocery retailers in Asia for the period 2014 to 2020. Over that same period, OECD/FAO forecast that total dairy consumption in the world would grow by 12%. Growth in Asia was expected to grow by 21% compared to 4% in Europe and 12% in North America, with the result that dairy demand in the coming years will be dominated by Asia. Farmer intentions survey 2015 by Luke Crossman, Senior Analyst, AHDB Market Intelligence The levy body for Great Britain (GB) undertakes an annual survey of dairy farmers to investigate the level of confidence in their own farming businesses and the industry generally, and in doing so identifies production and investment intentions. The 2015 survey covered 850 dairy farmers representative of herd size by region. The results showed that the position at the start of 2015 was a complete reversal of the previous year. Farm gate prices were around 20% lower than the year before and global supply was outstripping demand. The outcome was that there would be pressure on prices in the short term, but according to the report, the long-term message was positive. It was emphasised that in recent years, there has been a wide variation in farm gate prices. For example, at the end of 2013, there was a 3.37ppl difference between the top and bottom of the price league table, whilst at the end of 2014, the difference was 11.93ppl. In general, the survey showed that short term confidence had taken a knock. Yet one third of those surveyed planned to expand milk production in the next 2 years. Of those farmers who stated they intended to invest, they would do so largely in infrastructure, with 62% and 46% planning investments in farm buildings and equipment, respectively. Some 6% planned to leave the industry, up two per cent since the 2013 survey. Since the survey was carried out (December 2014), milk price had suffered further reductions which, it was suggested, could have a negative influence on producer intentions and so the survey results should be interpreted with caution. However, in the longer term, five years plus, dairy farmers were relatively confident about their business prospects and also about the industry generally, as the global long-term demand for dairy products was positive. Sustainable dairy production in the Netherlands by Maarten Vrolijk, Researcher System Innovation, Livestock Research, Wageningen In the final presentation, the structure of the dairy industry in the Netherlands (NL) was outlined, and as with the previous AHDB presentation, the attitudes and future expectations of farmers were explored. As in most parts of the global dairy industry, a key driver was the future global population increase and concomitant increased food demand, predicted to rise by 1% per year. As consumers became more affluent, they were expected to require more protein in their diets, and in relation to milk, global demand was forecast to increase by 50% by 2050. There was a double challenge ahead for the NL food industry as the speaker emphasised: ‘feeding the world within the carrying capacity of planet earth’. In an outline of the challenges facing NL farmers, the need to reduce carbon emissions and dispose of excess manure were serious environmental issues, whilst high land prices, rising feed costs and milk price volatility could limit investment. European Union policy changes including the removal of milk quotas in April 2015, likely lower direct payments and tough environmental regulations would also affect business planning. Overproduction was a future possibility with the result that the number of dairy cows could be restricted in the coming years. Yet in spite of all the challenges, the speaker reported that NL dairy farmers had faith in the future of the industry. The increase in world demand linked to having strong processors with established export expertise gave the industry confidence. The NL industry focus would be on a sustainable dairy chain including the building of more sustainable production plants, decrease water usage and reuse of energy and water, and making greater use of wind and solar energy. However, concern was expressed that some of the current traditional farming systems would not be able to meet future challenges. New skills plus a radical shift in the approach to building design, husbandry and management, was required to meet the future needs of government policy, environment and consumers. The Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board is a levy board funded by the agriculture and horticulture industries through statutory levies. Its role is to make the industry sectors it supports more competitive and sustainable. This annual conference was staged by the three divisions representing pigs, dairy, and beef and sheep. The conference was attended by a wide range of representatives from all livestock sectors and the food industry and provided valuable economic analyses and forecasting information to help delegates with future business planning. Copies of the presentation can be found at www.eblex.org.uk/events/conference-2015/outlook-2015 and for further information on this annual conference contact Claire Sayers-Smith at [email protected]

title: Food Price Elasticities for Policy Interventions: Estimates from a Virtual Supermarket Experiment in a Multistage Demand Analysis with (Expert) Prior Information
abstract: Food price elasticities (PEs) are essential for evaluating the impacts of food pricing interventions to improve dietary and health outcomes. This paper innovates the use of experimental purchasing data from a recent New Zealand virtual supermarket experiment to estimate PEs for a large set of disaggregated foods across major food groups relevant for food policies in a Bayesian multistage demand framework. We propose the use of available prior information to elicit prior demand parameter assumptions that are consistent with published PEs and economic assumptions and are weighted according to expert knowledge, increasing precision in PE inference and policy predictions, and yielding somewhat stronger price effects.

title: Millet Grains: Nutritional Quality, Processing, and Potential Health Benefits
abstract: Abstract In the 21st century, climate changes, water scarcity, increasing world population, rising food prices, and other socioeconomic impacts are expected to generate a great threat to agriculture and food security worldwide, especially for the poorest people who live in arid and subarid regions. These impacts present a challenge to scientists and nutritionists to investigate the possibilities of producing, processing, and utilizing other potential food sources to end hunger and poverty. Cereal grains are the most important source of the world's food and have a significant role in the human diet throughout the world. As one of the most important drought‐resistant crops, millet is widely grown in the semiarid tropics of Africa and Asia and constitutes a major source of carbohydrates and proteins for people living in these areas. In addition, because of their important contribution to national food security and potential health benefits, millet grain is now receiving increasing interest from food scientists, technologists, and nutritionists. The aim of this work was to review the recent advances in research carried out to date for purposes of evaluation of nutritional quality and potential health benefits of millet grains. Processing technologies used for improving the edible and nutritional characteristics of millet as well as challenges, limitations, and future perspectives to promote millet utilization as food for a large and growing population are also discussed.

title: Recent Advances in Food Drying Modeling: Empirical to Multiscale Physics‐Informed Neural Networks
abstract: Food insecurity is a major global challenge. Food preservation, particularly through drying, presents a promising solution to enhance food security and minimize waste. Fruits and vegetables contain 80%-90% water, and much of this is removed during drying. However, structural changes across multiple length scales occur during drying, compromising stability and affecting quality. Understanding these changes is essential, and several modeling techniques exist to analyze them, including empirical modeling, physics-based computational methods, purely data-driven machine learning approaches, and physics-informed neural network (PINN) models. Although empirical methods are straightforward to implement, their limited generalizability and lack of physical insights have led to the development of physics-based computational methods. These methods can achieve high spatiotemporal resolution without requiring experimental investigations. However, their complexity and high computational costs have prompted the exploration of data-driven machine learning models for drying processes, which involve comparatively lower computational costs and are more straightforward to execute. Nonetheless, their poor predictive ability with sparse data has restricted their application, leading to a hybrid modeling approach: PINN, which merges physical insights with data-driven machine learning techniques. This method still holds significant potential for advancements in food drying modeling. Therefore, this study aims to conduct a comprehensive literature review of state-of-the-art conventional drying modeling techniques, such as empirical, physics-based computational, and pure data-driven machine learning techniques, and explores the potential of the PINN approach for overcoming the limitations associated with conventional drying modeling strategies.

title: Household vulnerability to food price increases: the 2008 crisis in urban Southern Africa
abstract: Abstract Volatile food prices represent a common hazard to the food security of poor urban households. In trying to understand the impact of this hazard, income poverty is widely accepted as the principal predictive variable. But could other variables be important in understanding household vulnerability to food price shocks? This analysis uses survey data collected from 11 cities in Southern Africa by the African Food Security Urban Network during the 2008 food price crisis. As expected, the data show that household income is a significant predictor of the negative impact of rising food prices on household food security. However, other variables are significant predictors of household vulnerability to food insecurity as a result of food price increases. The analysis demonstrated how these diverse variables facilitated our classification of different households according to food price shocks using a CHAID decision tree. Demonstrating that household income is not the only significant predictor of household vulnerability to food price volatility, these findings broaden our understanding of the complex factors that can predispose households to food insecurity in the context of rising food prices.

title: Time to Resurrect Buffer Stocks?
abstract: Summary Volatile food prices create problems for consumers and farmers the world over. Buffer stocks offer a way out. A buffer stock is a quantity of grain owned by the government which sets a price band via a maximum price and a minimum price for grain. By buying and selling grain from the buffer stock on the open market, the government can keep the domestic price within its desired price band and thus avoid unstable prices. A buffer stock does not require the government to forecast the future price of grain and is entirely compatible with a market economy; the government is effectively exploiting the forces of supply and demand to influence the market price. A buffer stock is also compatible with free international trade. In using a buffer stock to stabilise its domestic price of grain, a government helps to stabilise the world price. In contrast, a government which resorts to trade measures to stabilise its domestic price can cause the world price to become less stable. In this article it is argued that all countries – rich and poor alike – would do their consumers, their farmers and the world as a whole a favour if they were to set up buffer stocks.

title: The Impact of the War in Ukraine on Food Security
abstract: The Food and Agricultural Organisation (FAO) defines food security as the situation where people have physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food that meets their dietary needs and preferences for an active and healthy life at all times; in other pwords, people are free from hunger and malnutrition (FAO, 2000). Food security has a number of pillars: it is about availability of, access to, use and stability of the food supply. In the 1970s, the focus of definitions of food security was mainly on food availability. Over time, the definition has been expanded to include aspects such as quality, nutritional value and access. When analysing food security, it is important to distinguish between the availability of food and access to it. After all, a great deal of food insecurity comes not as the result of food shortages, but as a consequence of lack of access. Poverty is the main cause of limited access to food: people simply do not have the money to buy it. The quality of food can also be a major obstacle to achieving food security; people may have access to sufficient calories, but the nutritional value – in terms of micro and macronutrients – is lacking. In this article I consider the impact of the war in Ukraine on global food security. Ukraine is a major exporter of wheat (18 mtonnes), maize (27.9 mtonnes), sunflower oil (6.8 mtonnes) and rapeseed (2.4 mtonnes) per annum (2020 UN Comtrade, www.comtrade.un.org). It has a substantial share of international trade for these crops as shown in Figure 1. Russia is also a major exporter of wheat and sunflower seed and oil (Figure 1). The largest importers of Ukrainian wheat are Egypt, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Turkey and Yemen. Russia exports its wheat mainly to Egypt and Turkey. These two countries are therefore heavily dependent on both Ukraine and Russia together for their wheat imports (Figure 2) and have limited possibilities to expand their wheat production (Meijl et al., 2022). All these importing countries also depend on food aid supplied through the World Food Programme (WFP). Ukraine is the largest supplier of food aid to the WFP. Source: UN Comtrade, International Trade Statistics database: https://comtrade.un.org As exports from Ukraine came to a halt following the Russian invasion on 24 February 2022, countries were forced to source their wheat elsewhere, at considerably higher prices due to the disruption of supply. Global wheat prices have gone up sharply since the Russian invasion, as well as prices of other food products (Figure 3). Note that food prices have been on the rise for a longer period due to a combination of factors, such as Covid disruptions to trade, economic recovery from the pandemic in 2021, and product specific causes, including droughts and the large-scale outbreak of African swine fever in China. Sharply increasing energy costs since the second half of 2021 have also played an important role. Source: FAOSTAT. Source: UN Comtrade, International Trade Statistics database: https://comtrade.un.org The FAO's latest estimate of the global stock-to-use ratios is 38.9 per cent for wheat and 24.4 per cent for coarse grains (FAO, 2022). A stock-to-use ratio of 20 per cent is regarded as a minimum for stocks to play their roles as buffers. The real food security problem is that poorer countries simply lack the money now to buy cereals, due to sharp increases in prices. This is aggravated by current export restrictions imposed by several countries, such as India for wheat flour and Indonesia for palm oil, that lead to even tighter markets and hence higher prices. Currently, the war in Ukraine and the ensuing food crisis is primarily an issue of access to food for a number of countries highly dependent on imports from Ukraine. The Russia-Ukraine agreement, signed on 22 July 2022 and enabling exports of grain from a number of ports in Ukraine, may alleviate the situation if the exports reach the countries most in need. However, there is much uncertainty as the deal could be disrupted by Russia at any time. In the next growing season, the crisis could become a wider spread issue of food availability if prices of energy and fertiliser inputs remain high. This could trigger farmers to use (much) fewer inputs, leading to lower output levels particularly in developing countries. For the medium (6 months-2 years) to long term (>2 years), there is a great deal of uncertainty about the impact of the war on food security. This involves both the direct consequences of the war and the consequences of sanctions being and yet to be imposed on Russia. More than ever it is important that the international community works together to prevent any worsening of the food security situation.

title: The Global Dimension of the CAP Debate: Between a Rock and a Hard Place
abstract: Summary Exuberant expectations about what EU agriculture can and should deliver in policy areas beyond its scope often contrast sharply with both farm realities and contradictions in the behaviour of individuals as citizens and consumers. This has polarised the CAP policy debate, and erroneously pushes for a choice between prioritising either climate action or food security. Recent developments, including the war in Ukraine, added to concerns about uncertain and volatile future price prospects. Food price prospects and population growth impacts are pivotal in the debate about food security as higher food costs, prospects for higher energy costs driven by the green transition and increasing income inequalities put households in both developed and the developing world at risk with respect to food affordability. Adding trends of global population growth, especially in Africa, creates a clear challenge of availability in certain products and regions. The EU's underestimated and misunderstood record of producing more with less could help EU agriculture to positively contribute to addressing both food security and climate change. However, further improving its performance requires re‐opening the debate in three priority areas where the EU must come clear on its stance and future contribution – productivity, science and trade.

title: Food security, food systems and food sovereignty in the 21st century: A new paradigm required to meet S ustainable D evelopment G oals
abstract: '… We envisage a world free of poverty, hunger, disease and want, where all life can thrive. We envisage a world free of fear and violence. A world with universal literacy. A world with equitable and universal access to quality education at all levels, to health care and social protection, where physical, mental and social well-being are assured. A world where we reaffirm our commitments regarding the human right to safe drinking water and sanitation and where there is improved hygiene; and where food is sufficient, safe, affordable and nutritious. A world where human habitats are safe, resilient and sustainable and where there is universal access to affordable, reliable and sustainable energy.' In the current socio-political climate, these words may sound like the opening to a fairy tale. They are, in fact, an excerpt from the vision of the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs),1 recently endorsed by heads of state and government, and high representatives at the United Nations (UN) headquarters in New York. It is noteworthy that the 2015 meeting at which the SDGs were affirmed also marked the 70th anniversary of the UN. The SDGs follow on from the Millenium Development Goals (MDGs)2 that were adopted by world leaders at the Millennium Summit held in September 2000. The MDGs were quantified targets for addressing extreme poverty in its many dimensions, including income poverty, hunger, disease, lack of adequate shelter and exclusion—while at the same time, promoting gender equality, education and environmental sustainability. By 2015, progress towards meeting the MDGs had been uneven.3 Notably, in Africa and least developed countries, some of the MDGs remain off-track, in particular those related to maternal, newborn and child health and to reproductive health. Through the SDGs, the UN recommits itself to the full realisation of all the MDGs, including the off-track ones, by providing focussed and scaled-up assistance to least developed nations, in line with relevant support programmes. The SDGs seek to complete what the MDGs did not achieve, particularly in reaching the most vulnerable. Importantly, the SDGs hold all countries to account. The seventeen SDGs, with their 169 associated targets, focus on human rights—the rights of each person on the planet to food, health, education, shelter and security—as well as equity. The goals and targets represent a supremely ambitious and transformational vision which will require cooperation not only between governments of different countries and regions, both north and south, but also between sectors such as agriculture, health, technology, economic development and climate change. The global issues of hunger, food poverty and undernutrition are common themes within both the MDGs and their successor SDGs. In the context of food security, the SDGs challenge nutrition professionals and policy makers to think broadly about potential solutions that encompass non-traditional approaches. Accessibility (physical and economic access to food) The review will also consider training and educational needs for public health nutritionists and dietitians to become competent in this complex and multidimensional area of practice. Food security is commonly defined as the physical, social and economic ability to access sufficient, safe and nutritious food.5, 6 The four pillars of food security that are intrinsic to this definition are availability of food, stability of the food supply, access to adequate food and utilisation of food (Table 1). While not always explicit, each pillar contains nutrition considerations and components crucial to the links in the chain between national food economies, households and individual well-being. Undernourishment may be considered 'an extreme form of food insecurity', defined as the state 'when caloric intake is below the minimum dietary energy requirement'.7 Hunger, on the other hand, may be described as 'the uneasy or painful sensation caused by a lack of food … the recurrent and involuntary lack of access to food'.8 'Hidden hunger' is the term used to refer to micronutrient deficiencies which affect around 2 billion people worldwide.7 The term nutrition security is sometimes used interchangeably with food insecurity,6 but in fact the definition is much broader. Food security is necessary, but not sufficient for nutrition security.6 Nutrition security considers care, health, and hygiene practices in addition to food security. The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) defines nutrition security as 'A situation that exists when secure access to an appropriately nutritious diet is coupled with a sanitary environment, adequate health services and care, in order to ensure a healthy and active life for all household members'.7 It has been proposed that the two terms should be brought together as 'food and nutrition security' to better reflect the importance of nutrition's role in sustainable food security and make the explicit distinction between quantity (energy) and quality (dietary diversity) at the individual level. In this regard, the conceptual framework proposed by the Food Insecurity and Vulnerability Information and Mapping System (FIVIMS)9 provides a useful guide for intervention points for inter-sectoral nutrition activities to address food insecurity (Figure 1). FIVIMS is an inter-agency initiative, with FAO acting as a secretariat, set up to monitor progress in achieving the World Food Summit goal for eradicating hunger and achieving food security. Similar to the UNICEF conceptual framework for causes of malnutrition10, 11 in women and children, the FIVIMS model includes health and care components but includes all population sectors, with specific emphasis on the role of the food economy. The FIVIMS framework promotes food and agriculture-based strategies to increase access to and consumption of adequately diversified diets. However, it also takes cognisance of the fact that improved availability, stability and access to food at aggregate levels does not necessarily imply improved energy and nutrient intake at individual levels. The inter-connectedness between links in the chain is clearly demonstrated by this framework. Food and Agriculture Organization/Food Insecurity and Vulnerability Information and Mapping System framework of food security: Development context, food economy, household and individual level impacts.9 Reprinted with permission from FAO.9 (Available from: http://www.fao.org/fileadmin/user_upload/fsn/docs/FIVIMS_Framework_of_Food_Security.pdf, accessed 23 December 2015). There is little doubt that poverty is the major contributor to food insecurity. It is estimated that 1.2 billion people live in extreme poverty and about 870 million are undernourished globally.12 Strategies to improve livelihoods and income of the poorest sectors of communities are essential to achieve food security for all. Who is at risk of food insecurity in Australia? While Australia and other OECD countries may enjoy a relatively high standard of living, and there is widespread availability of sufficient food, in terms of quantity, there is evidence that some sectors are unable to access healthy foods required for a nutritious diet. The affordability of food can be assessed by costing a specific selection of healthy items, and expressed as a percentage of total household income. Information collected using healthy food basket surveys can be compared against the Consumer Price Index (CPI) for the same period, to account for changes in inflation and to assess relative affordability of nutritious foods. There are a number of healthy food basket surveys conducted across states and territories in Australia. While specific food items included within the various basket surveys may differ slightly, they generally reflect the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating. For example, the biennial Illawarra Healthy Food Basket survey that has collected data since 2000 consists of a basket of 57 foods, designed to meet the weekly nutritional requirements of a family of five in the region. The healthy food basket cost $345 per week in 2011, representing a 71% increase from 2000, which was equivalent to 34% of average weekly earnings, or 36% of welfare payments. Over a 10-year period between 2000 and 2010, increases in the cost of a healthy food basket remained in line with the CPI, as well as with increases in average weekly earnings and welfare benefits, which indicates that healthy food choices remained affordable.13 However, disproportionate increases in fruit and vegetable prices during that time period made healthy food choices difficult for low income families. Even within one local government area, prices of healthy food baskets can differ. In Victoria, accessibility to healthy food decreased significantly between inner, middle and outer suburbs, with outer suburbs using proportionately more of their income on the food basket.14 Food prices are known to be even higher in remote and rural locations where residents may rely largely on a single local store for food purchases and may have limited food choices, in terms of variety and quality, particularly for fresh produce, accompanied by transportation difficulties. In these areas, the cost of healthy foods has risen more than the cost of some less nutritious foods, making the latter relatively more affordable. In Queensland, in 2010, the cost of the Healthy Food Access Basket in very remote areas was 26–31% higher than in major cities, while the cost of fruit, vegetables and legumes in the basket was 35–38% higher.15, 16 In Northern Territory communities, 34% of the family income is needed to purchase a healthy food basket17 in remote stores, compared to 22% in the major city of Darwin. On average, the food basket in remote stores was 53% more expensive than in the city. Indigenous Australians living with disabilities in rural and remote areas are considered to be at particularly high risk of food insecurity. A qualitative study conducted in the West Kimberley region of Western Australia identified that food insecurity is extremely complex for this group.18 Participants reported that in times of economic stress, food is the first commodity that aboriginal people with disabilities would forgo. One of the proposed 'Close the Gap' equity targets is for 90% of indigenous families to be able to access a healthy food basket for under 25% of their income by 2018.19 Progress towards this goal is slow. In the most recent Australian National Nutrition Survey (2011–2012),20 more than one in five (22%) aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people were living in a household that, in the previous 12 months, had run out of food and had not been able to afford to buy more. This was dramatically higher than food insecurity reported in the non-indigenous population (3.7%)21 which demonstrates wide inequities in the country. Older adults are another sector of the population who may be at high risk of food insecurity and may have significant adverse health outcomes associated with being food insecure. Population ageing in all regions of the world will result in an increase in the number of older adults living to advanced ages and present a burden to already stretched health and social services. In low-middle income countries, most adults enter old age after a lifetime of poverty and deprivation, poor access to health care and a diet that is usually inadequate in quantity and quality.22 Even in a middle-upper income country that provides a non-contributory old age social pension, households that are headed by older persons experience higher food insecurity than those headed by younger persons, except in the case of small households comprising one or two people who do not need to share their pension with other family members.22 The adverse impact of being food insecure on health and quality of life has been demonstrated in the Australian Blue Mountains Eye cohort study (n = 2642). Using a comprehensive 12-item food security instrument, those older adults that were classified as being food insecure had worse reported physical and mental health status.23 People on special diets may too be at risk of inadequate intakes because of increased costs associated with their therapeutic diet. Lambert and colleagues24 report that, compared to a regular healthy food basket, a gluten free option was considered unaffordable for three of the four common family types in regional Australia. Families on welfare who have a member requiring a gluten free diet may be particularly vulnerable to food insecurity. The authors propose creation of a national subsidised medical foods program to enable equitable access to affordable gluten free staple foods via prescription. Migrants, asylum seekers and refugees are vulnerable to food insecurity, particularly when they first arrive in their country of settlement.25-28 The principle exacerbating factor is the delay in receipt of benefits.26 Other causes include inadequate income, feeding children first, feeling shame over using emergency relief, inadequate access to emergency relief, lack of culturally appropriate foods and the psychological consequence of the refugee experience. In order to develop culturally appropriate programs to increase health and nutrition literacy, and thereby improve food and nutrition security among migrant groups, insights into perceptions about their health-seeking behaviours are required. A qualitative study of sub-Saharan African migrants residing in Melbourne identified three distinct themes with regard to perceptions related to diabetes.29 Participants did not pay much attention to the threat of type 2 diabetes, considered the disease to be outside of their control and being a disease associated with culture and life style of rich industrialised countries. Diabetes was regarded as a disease of the wealthy, caused by intake of too much sugar and sedentary behaviour. Development of strategies to address the needs of different sectors of the population that are at highest risk of food insecurity will require consideration of the underlying determinants of inadequate food intake in each of these groups. Poverty alleviation and economic development is core to addressing the needs of low income families, indigenous communities and migrants and refugees. However, changes to the food system including food pricing and infrastructure (roads and transport) are needed for those living in remote and rural areas, while older adults may require social services support in order to maintain an adequate dietary intake. Solving the world's food insecurity problem requires a far-reaching comprehensive strategy that includes consideration of biodiversity and sustainability. The debate is no longer just about producing enough food, but also about ensuring equity and access, including for future generations. This is not a new message. Over a decade ago, the New Nutrition Science project30 identified the need for a conceptual framework that incorporated social and environmental dimensions into the biological construct of nutrition science. The new nutrition science was concerned with personal and population health, but also with planetary health—a revolutionary concept at the time, and one which left nutrition professionals feeling uncomfortable and ill equipped. Climate change is now front and foremost of the sustainability debate, with firm commitment under the Paris climate agreement from 195 countries to take action to limit the global temperature rise to below 2°C. This will require reductions in greenhouse gas emissions of between 40% and 70% by 2050 and complete decarbonisation of the world economy by 2100.31 Australia had already stated that it will reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 26–28% by 2030 compared to 2005 levels.32 But under the Paris agreement, this is insufficient. Emission reductions of 4% each year to 2050 are needed—which represents approximately 45% reductions by 2030. One of the key differences between the 2015 Paris agreement and that of the Clean Development Mechanism of the 1997 Kyoto Protocol33 is the lack of a formal distinction between the responsibility of developed (upper income) and developing (lower-middle income) countries. The new mechanism intends to support new policies, activities and programs such as financial support to improve energy efficiency in the building sector of a country or to introduce and implement a renewable energy policy. Notably, the new mechanism requires a reduction in global emissions, rather than simply offsetting emissions. Many of the proposed changes relate to the energy production sector, with a move from fossil fuels (coal) to renewable energy mechanisms. It remains to be seen how agricultural and farming practices, both large and small-scale, will need to change to contribute to significant carbon reductions. Changes to the food systems of countries, combined with individual pro-environmental dietary choices, also have the potential to contribute to reduced carbon and mitigation of climate change. The environmental impact of food commodities has attracted much attention, and no food more so than beef. This is because beef cattle have low efficiency in converting natural resources to edible products and require higher water use and land use than any other livestock systems.34 Beef supply chains are estimated to emit about 40% of all livestock greenhouse gas emissions, using a life-cycle approach.35 Reducing the consumption of meat and increasing the proportion that is derived from the most efficient sources offer an opportunity to feed more people. abstract: I have a Twitter account that I use to track food science and agriculture news. It has also allowed me to make contacts with several food technologists and aspiring food technologists. I was recently in contact with a food science student in Indonesia. This student is competing in this year's IFTSA Developing Solutions for Developing Countries Competition. The Developing Solutions competition promotes the application of food science and technology and the development of new products and processes that are targeted at improving the quality of life for people in developing countries. It is a great way for food science students to do product development by applying what they are learning. The theme for the competition is based on real-world challenges. The 2017–2018 theme: “Two consecutive years of drought in South and East Africa have resulted in rising food prices and increased food insecurity and malnutrition. With more than 38 million people affected by this drought, sustainable solutions are needed to combat these challenges. Develop a product using primarily drought-tolerant crops for people living in one of the affected countries.” The entries must consist of a proposal for a new concept readily applicable to food or water in developing countries. This may include, but is not limited to, concepts such as a new food product, microbiological/chemical/biochemical method, distribution system, packaging material, food delivery system, nutrient fortification concept, or the new use of local ingredients for a safer, more nutritious product. Because the competition is team-based, it allows more students to participate. However, at least one team member must hold student member status in IFT at the time of the submission of the preliminary report. All finalist team members must be current IFT student members. Multiple teams may participate from the same chapter or University. The deadline for the 2017–2018 competition is January 15. But, if you are a student or food science teacher, you should consider this competition next year. I'm looking forward to this year's entries and all the best luck to the team of my Twitter friend from Indonesia! For more about this competition, see https://www.ift.org/community/students/competitions/developing-solutions-for-developing-countries.aspx Highlights in this issue include testing a sensory flip from meat-centric to plant-centric diets; using chia as a substitute for oil or egg yolk in mayonnaise; characterizing peanut oil bodies; using an edible coating for cherry tomatoes; and profiling peppers. The American diet is lacking in plant-based foods and vegetables, higher in protein than necessary, and too centered on meat and poultry. Two major dietary shifts recommended by the 2015–2020 U.S. Dietary Guidelines are to increase vegetable intake and to increase the variety of protein food sources. One suggested strategy for doing this is to partially replace meat and poultry with vegetables and plant-based ingredients in mixed dishes. These researchers tested the potential of flavor modalities (taste, aroma, trigeminal, and their combination) as strategies to increase the sensory appeal of plant-forward dishes. Three factors were tested: cuisine (Latin American, Mediterranean, and Asian), meat proportion (high-meat/low-vegetable versus low-meat/high-vegetable), and flavor strategy (taste, aroma, trigeminal, and a reduced-intensity trimodal combination). Four consumer preference segments were uncovered. The low-meat dishes achieved parity or higher in consumer acceptance across all recipes and flavor strategies. This research provides insight into consumer preferences regarding flavor strategies to partially replace meat with vegetables in mixed dishes. The research explores various flavor and culinary strategies with which to carry out the mixed dish meat-vegetable swap and to test the potential of the Flexitarian Flip™ (the shift from meat-centric to plant-centric diets). This research shows that individuals have different preferences regarding the type of flavor they prefer in mixed dishes (for example, some consumers prefer salty and some prefer spicy), so if the dietitian can recommend recipes that cater to that client's food and flavor preferences, the client will be more likely to adhere to their diet. 175–187 Native to southern Mexico and northern Guatemala, the chia seed can be a rich source of essential fatty acids, dietary fiber, and proteins. In the presence of water, the chia seed exudes a transparent mucilaginous gel, composed essentially of soluble fibers. This gel is called chia mucilage and features some useful characteristics as a texture modifier, gelling agent, thickener, stabilizer, emulsifier, and bulking agent when incorporated in foods These researchers explored the use of chia mucilage to substitute oil and egg yolk in mayonnaise, aiming to reduce the lipid content and increase the nutritional value of the product, making it healthier. In the study, mayonnaises were prepared with different levels of freeze-dried chia mucilage instead of oil or egg yolk. The substitution of oil in mayonnaise promoted increased stability and texture parameters, and the mayonnaise substituted by egg yolk presented similar stability and texture parameters as the control mayonnaise. Sensory testing results indicated that chia mucilage has potential to substitute part of the amount of oil in the mayonnaise formulation. However, as for the use of the mucilage in the substitution of the egg yolk, it is not possible to promote a significant reduction in the lipid content nor maintain emulsion stability. The researchers believe that chia mucilage presents high emulsifying ability and water-holding capacity and that it could be used as a substitute for fat in various foods. Mayonnaises developed with up to 45% oil substitution by chia mucilage, presented a reduction in the lipid content by about 50%, an increasing stability, and a good sensorial acceptance. 74–83 Peanut is an incredibly rich source of oil and proteins and contains around 44% to 56% oil and 22% to 30% proteins. It is widely consumed as peanut butter, peanut biscuit, and in its raw form. Still, more than 50% of peanut is used only for extraction of edible oil. Peanut oil is rich in unsaturated fatty acids, representing 80%. Peanut is also free from trans-fats and rich in vitamin E and phytosterols. These researchers explored the major compounds, lipids, and proteins as well as nutritive compounds such as vitamin E and phytosterols within peanut oil bodies using the aqueous extraction method at different pH. The results showed that peanut oil bodies are rich in nutritional components such as essential amino acids, unsaturated fatty acids, vitamin E, and phytosterols. Moreover, the oil bodies are surrounded with two oleosin isoforms and caleosin, which offer more stability to the emulsion system. The researchers believe that the peanut oil bodies could be perfect for foods like mayonnaise and vinaigrettes products in the form of encapsulated oil with high content of vitamin E. 93–100 Being a climacteric fruit, cherry tomato ripens and senesces rapidly after harvest owing to transpiration and respiration, and is easily damaged and contaminated by microorganisms. In this study, the researchers wanted to develop a chitosan-based grapefruit-seed-extract-incorporating edible coating for application to cherry tomato; and investigate the effects of the coating on microbiological safety against Salmonella, physicochemical properties, and sensory attributes of cherry tomatoes stored at 10 and 25 °C. Grapefruit seed extract (GSE)-containing chitosan-based coating were developed and applied to cherry tomatoes to protect them from Salmonella invasion and improve their storability. The coating colloids were produced by mixing a chitosan colloid with GSE at various concentrations using high-shear mixing. Their results indicated that a novel chitosan coating containing grapefruit seed extract improved microbiological safety against Salmonella and storability of cherry tomatoes without altering their flavor, demonstrating its strong potential as an effective postharvest technology. A chitosan coating containing GSE might be preferable over chitosan coating without GSE for application to tomatoes that are stored at room temperature, in that it more effectively inhibits microbial growth and weight loss than the coating without GSE at 25 °C. 138–146 Peppers are traditionally used in Korea as a fermented paste, a spice, and a major ingredient of “kimchi”, which is made of fermented Chinese cabbage or other vegetables. They are consumed both in the immature stage as well as in the mature stages, in which the pepper changes color from green to red as it ripens. Maturity is associated with changes in the levels of carotenoids, tocopherols, and phytosterols. These researchers analyzed the primary metabolites, carotenoids, tocopherols, sterols, policosanols, and free phenolic acids in five pepper cultivars and to determine the relationships among the amount of these metabolites and to understand their metabolic links. They determined the content of various metabolites, such as hydrophilic and lipophilic compounds, phenolic acids, carotenoids, and capsaicinoids in peppers of various colors (green, red, pale green, and violet peppers) and in a high-pungency (green) pepper. They also performed principal component analysis (PCA), Pearson's correlation analysis, and hierarchical clustering analysis (HCA) to determine the relationships among these metabolites in peppers. The PCA results indicated no significant variances among the three sample replicates. The HCA showed correlations between the metabolites resulting from common or closely-linked biosynthesis pathways. A total of 71 metabolites were measured in five peppers of different colors. The metabolic profiling with multivariate analysis revealed that tocopherol content had a positive correlation with the carotenoid content and a negative correlation with the phytosterol content. The results of this study may help in breeding programs to produce new germplasm with enhanced nutritional quality. 2885–2893 James Giese, jhgiese@gmail.com

abstract: The Journal of Food Science recently sent out a call for papers for a Special Issue on Artificial Intelligence in Food Science and Nutrition. This Special Issue should be compiled and posted sometime later this year. Artificial intelligence (AI) has many applications in the food industry, including food safety, product development, sensory evaluation, nutritional and health-related uses, and food security. In recent years, AI use in the food industry has attracted attention in many areas, including research into intelligence graphs, deep learning (DL), algorithms, language processing, development algorithms, machine learning (ML), and skilled systems. While AI has become a catch-all term in the media, in reality, there are differences between a Large Language Model (LLM) and Application-Specific AI (often called Narrow AI or Vertical AI), such as the ones for the food industry. The most obvious difference lies in what the AI is designed to do. LLMs (General Purpose) are trained on massive datasets covering almost every human topic. An LLM can write an essay or write Python code. They are flexible but can fail at application-specific tasks. Application-Specific AI (Narrow) is designed to excel at one specific task and nothing else. If an AI is controlling the temperature of a process, it uses deterministic logic or highly constrained statistical models that prioritize accuracy and repeatability over versatility. The main fields of AI in the food industry include robotics, expert systems, computer vision, DL, natural language processing, and ML. The development of AI in the food industry aims to save time, reduce labor, cut costs, increase production rates, improve the quality of final products, meet consumer demands, enhance nutritional value, create new food products, and boost overall food quantity. Enhancing food safety and traceability of food products in the food production industry is one of the major challenges. As a branch of AI, ML has been widely used to develop and refine algorithms and statistical models for food product development, sensory evaluation, and improving the quality and safety of final products. An example of AI in the food industry can be found in this month's highlights: “Enhancing Food Safety in the Cold Chain Through Internet of Things and Artificial Intelligence” by Wagner Augusto Müller, Sandro Binsfeld Ferreira, Suse Botelho da Silva (https://doi.org/10.1111/1750-3841.70871, the first article published for the special issue noted above) is a systematic review of 97 peer-reviewed studies (2010–2025) that highlight how the integration of Internet of Things (IoT) technologies and AI is reshaping food cold chain management. Traditional systems rely heavily on manual checks and fragmented temperature logging, often detecting problems only after product quality or safety has been compromised. In contrast, IoT-enabled sensors—tracking temperature, humidity, CO2, GPS location, and more—provide real-time visibility, while AI models convert those data streams into predictive insights that anticipate spoilage, contamination risk, and logistics disruptions. The review shows rapid growth in both IoT and AI adoption, driven by regulatory pressure, food waste concerns, and demand for traceability. Temperature sensors dominate current deployments, particularly in fruits, vegetables, meat, and seafood, but secondary sensors such as gas and humidity monitoring are increasingly used to capture early spoilage indicators. On the AI side, applications range from regression models for demand forecasting to advanced neural networks that predict product freshness, temperature deviations, or pathogen risk with high reported accuracy. Optimization algorithms are also being used to improve routing, reduce fuel use, and align delivery schedules with perishability profiles. The reviewers identify important gaps between laboratory performance and real-world deployment. Many AI models rely on limited or simulated datasets, raising concerns about generalizability under operational stress. Complex neural networks often lack interpretability, which complicates regulatory acceptance in food safety contexts where auditability is critical. IoT systems face their own challenges, including cybersecurity vulnerabilities, sensor drift, interoperability barriers, and the high upfront costs that can limit adoption among small and mid-sized operators. Looking ahead, the most promising direction is the development of closed-loop systems—where IoT sensors continuously feed data to AI models that automatically adjust refrigeration settings, reroute shipments, or trigger targeted interventions in real time. While most current implementations remain open-loop (monitoring only) or advisory (human action required), the review argues that integrating edge computing, explainable AI, and standardized data frameworks will be key to building resilient, transparent, and predictive cold chains. Additional highlights of studies published in the Journal of Food Science during the past month address many areas such as consumer acceptance, food security, food nutrition, food production sustainability, and food safety: Rice flour bread often suffers from low loaf volume and a firm, dense crumb because it lacks gluten's elastic network. In this study, researchers evaluated egg white (EW) as a functional improver in a rice flour–EW composite system designed to mimic breadmaking and determine why loaf quality changes. Thermal analysis showed that EW increased the system's thermal stability and helped suppress starch retrogradation—an important driver of staling and crumb firming in gluten-free breads. Rheology results indicated that EW also restrained starch swelling and shifted viscoelastic behavior: at 9% (w/w) EW, both storage (Gʹ) and loss (Gʺ) moduli reached their lowest values, while creep compliances (Jm and Jmax) peaked, reflecting a more fluid system with a weakened rigid structure. In practical terms, EW acted largely as an “inert filler” that reduced stiffness while changing how the dough deforms under stress. Microscopic interpretation suggested EW proteins occupy interstitial spaces between starch granules, improving dough continuity and, crucially, boosting gas retention during proofing/baking. That translated into better finished bread performance, including higher specific volume, lower hardness, and a more uniform crumb structure—suggesting EW as a targeted strategy for improving gluten-free rice bread quality. https://doi.org/10.1111/1750-3841.70666 These researchers affiliated with Kansas State University in Manhattan, Kansas, USA, examined how ethnocentrism influences Indians’ willingness to buy imported foods—and what price premiums shoppers assign based on country of origin. Using an online survey of 630 consumers, researchers tested five commonly purchased items in India (bananas, milk, lentils, potatoes, and namkeen) sourced from 13 countries, including India, the United States, Australia, New Zealand, China, and others. Respondents reported both willingness to buy and the price they were willing to pay for each product-country pairing. Ethnocentric attitudes were measured using the generalized ethnocentrism scale, then analyzed via exploratory factor analysis and segmented using hierarchical and k-means clustering into high, moderate, and low ethnocentrism groups. Even with these differing levels, a clear pattern emerged: consumers collectively preferred domestically produced foods and were willing to pay the highest premium for “Made in India” options across categories. Imported products from developed countries—particularly Australia, the United States, and New Zealand—were viewed more favorably than most other foreign sources but still ranked behind domestic foods. China stood out as the least favorable origin among the 13 countries evaluated, indicating that country-of-origin perceptions can significantly shape acceptance even before quality or brand cues enter the picture. Demographics helped explain who holds stronger ethnocentric beliefs. Income had the largest influence, followed by education level, gender, and age. For food marketers, the findings point to a practical product segmentation playbook. Messaging should align with local-production cues for ethnocentric segments, while positioning select imported origins as “trusted, premium alternatives” for less ethnocentric or more globally oriented consumers. For policymakers, the results reinforce the strategic value of strengthening domestic supply and leveraging “Made in India” initiatives to match consumer preference with national production goals. https://doi.org/10.1111/1750-3841.70919 A new survey and lab analysis of industrial fruit-processing byproducts in Sri Lanka highlights a sizable—and largely underused—stream of nutrient- and bioactive-rich materials. Across four major processors, pineapple, mango, papaya, and passion fruit were identified as the most heavily processed fruits, generating high waste yields of roughly half to more than two-thirds of incoming fruit mass. These residues were primarily peels, seeds, and bagasse, underscoring just how much potential raw material is available for upcycling into value-added food and nutraceutical ingredients. When the wastes were dehydrated and milled into powders, proximate composition varied widely by fruit fraction. Protein ranged from as low as ∼0.5% to as high as ∼25.9% (highest in papaya seed), fat spanned ∼0.36% to ∼28.2% (notably high in some seeds), and crude fiber reached ∼13%–43%, indicating strong potential for fiber enrichment applications. Mineral screening showed meaningful levels of essential elements such as potassium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, and copper across multiple waste types, supporting a positioning as nutrition-forward ingredients when properly formulated. The bioactive profile was equally notable. Total phenolics ranged from about 1.85 to 9.47 mg GAE/g, while flavonoids ranged from ∼1.38 to 21.82 mg RE/g. Antioxidant measures also varied substantially, with total antioxidant capacity spanning ∼1.85–25.54 mg AAE/g and DPPH scavenging performance (IC50) indicating particularly strong activity in mango and papaya peels and mango seed kernels—consistent with their higher phenolic and flavonoid levels. In practical terms, these fractions look especially promising as natural antioxidant sources for functional foods, extracts, or ingredient blends. From an industry standpoint, the work suggests prioritizing high-volume streams (pineapple peel/bagasse; mango peel/seed) and targeting applications that fit their strengths—fiber enrichment, antioxidant fortification, and nutraceutical ingredient development. The study also flags a key commercialization consideration. While toxic metals were mostly below permissible limits, lead exceeded recommended thresholds in some samples, reinforcing the need for robust sourcing, monitoring, and mitigation protocols before scaling food-grade uses. https://doi.org/10.1111/1750-3841.70938 Whey permeate powders (WPPs) are widely used dairy coproduct ingredients, but their tendency to cake, brown, and lose flowability during storage remains a persistent industry challenge. In this comprehensive study, researchers analyzed three commercial WPPs to establish their key “water relationships”—linking composition, structure, water activity, and glass transition behavior—and to explain why these powders are inherently unstable under typical storage conditions. Microscopy and x-ray diffraction supported a two-phase structural model: WPP particles contain crystalline α-lactose monohydrate and a distinct amorphous phase composed of residual lactose, organic acids (notably lactic acid), peptides, and minerals. Two dominant morphologies were observed—(1) small lactose crystals embedded in a continuous amorphous matrix and (2) large lactose crystals coated with a thin amorphous layer. Thermal analysis revealed that the amorphous phase exhibits a very low glass transition temperature (Tg), even at low water activities, and is strongly plasticized by moisture. Critically, the powders as received (aw ≈ 0.18–0.24) were already in the rubbery state at room temperature (25°C), explaining their high susceptibility to caking and browning during transport and storage. Modified Guggenheim–Anderson–de Boer equation (GAB) and Gordon–Taylor models, accounting for crystal-bound water in lactose monohydrate, showed that simply drying WPPs further offers limited stabilization potential. Even fully dried powders remain close to or below practical Tg thresholds because of the inherently low Tg of the amorphous fraction. In conclusion, the researchers state that stability is dictated less by total moisture and more by the composition and Tg of the amorphous phase. Increasing the Tg of this phase—rather than pursuing more aggressive drying—emerges as a more effective strategy to mitigate caking and color formation. By establishing water vapor sorption behavior and Tg as functions of both water content and water activity, this work provides a practical framework for defining safe storage conditions and guiding future formulation and processing interventions to improve WPP functionality. https://doi.org/10.1111/1750-3841.70883 Shrinkage—defined as post-hardening volume loss—is a persistent defect in high-protein, high-overrun frozen desserts, particularly under temperature-cycled storage. In this study, researchers evaluated formulations made with 6% milk protein concentrate (MPC), sodium caseinate (NaCN), or whey protein isolate (WPI), with and without 0.15% mono- and diglycerides (MDGs), at 100% and 150% overrun. By tracking ice crystal size, air cell size, fat destabilization, melting behavior, and volume loss over 6 weeks of temperature cycling, the researchers identified how microstructure and interfacial chemistry govern foam collapse and shrinkage. Across formulations, temperature cycling promoted ice recrystallization and air cell coarsening, but the magnitude depended strongly on protein source and MDG addition. MDGs significantly reduced ice crystal growth and, in MPC and WPI systems, increased fat destabilization by displacing proteins from the fat interface—creating a destabilized fat network that improved structural integrity. WPI with 0.15% MDGs and 150% overrun maintained the smallest ice crystals after 6 weeks and did not exceed the 50 µm sensory coarseness threshold. In contrast, NaCN systems showed minimal fat destabilization and different interfacial behavior, influencing both air stability and storage performance. Melting data indicated that fat destabilization was the strongest predictor of slower drip-through rates and better shape retention. Products with greater destabilized fat networks collapsed more slowly at room temperature, while those with weaker interfacial structures exhibited faster foam breakdown. However, shrinkage during frozen storage was not strongly predicted by ice crystal size alone. Instead, air phase destabilization—particularly gas diffusion, channel formation, and interfacial collapse—was the critical driver. Overall, the study demonstrates that shrinkage in high-protein frozen desserts is best understood as frozen foam collapse.
