title: Reproducibility Package for "Forecasting Food Inflation Risk across 194 Economies: Commodity Signals beyond Global Inflation"
abstract: This reproducibility package accompanies the study “Forecasting Food Inflation Risk across 194 Economies: Commodity Signals beyond Global Inflation.” The study evaluates whether commodity-specific global signals provide incremental predictive information for domestic food-inflation risk after local food-inflation dynamics and a broad measure of international inflation have already been incorporated into the forecasting information set. The empirical design covers 194 economies/countries/territories and uses a pseudo-real-time forecasting framework with primary horizons of 1, 3, and 6 months. The package contains checksum-verified research inputs, provenance metadata, fixed model configurations, executable Python code, machine-readable reference results, validation materials, and reproducibility checks supporting the analyses reported in the manuscript. The primary forecasting framework compares nested information sets I0–I3 using pooled Elastic Net and quantile HistGradientBoosting models. The main estimand is the within-model difference in forecast loss between I3 and I1, assessing whether global food, energy, fertilizer, and oil-price signals add predictive information after accounting for broad international inflation conditions. The reproducibility workflow supports the principal probabilistic forecasting analyses, including q10/q50/q90 forecasts, weighted interval scores (WIS), pinball loss, interval coverage and width, dependence-aware inference, income-group heterogeneity, regime analyses, robustness checks, and the tables and figures reported in the manuscript. The underlying source data are derived from FAOSTAT Food CPI and General CPI, the FAO Food Price Index, and the World Bank Commodity Price Data (Pink Sheet). Third-party source data remain subject to the terms, attribution requirements, licensing conditions, and applicable rights of their respective providers. Inclusion of provider-derived files in this package does not transfer ownership or relicense those data. Users should begin with README.md and START_HERE.md and consult RUN_GUIDE.md for environment setup, integrity verification, and reproduction instructions.

title: Performance Assessment, Decision Support, and Market Potential of Smart Irrigation Technologies
abstract: The agriculture sector is experiencing a quick transformation into a digitally intelligent state, which is facilitated by various challenges such as water shortage, climate variability, population expansion, and increased necessity to utilize resources in an effective manner without compromising food security. Irrigated agriculture accounts for about 70% of global freshwater use, and thus efficient irrigation management is crucial for the sustainable development of the agriculture sector. This chapter focuses on presenting a thorough review of methods and approaches related to performance evaluation methodologies, productivity assessment, economic analysis, decision support systems, digital advice, commercialization, market and investment possibilities associated with smart irrigation technologies. Recent advancements in precision irrigation management enabled through the Internet of Things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), remote sensing (RS), geographic information systems (GIS), cloud computing, and digital decision support systems have made irrigation management data-driven and predictive instead of being reactive in nature.

title: Replication package: Predicting Agricultural Supply Chain Disruption (18-country version)
abstract: Replication package for "Predicting Agricultural Supply Chain Disruption: A Machine Learning Approach Using Trade, Climate, and Production Data" (18-country revision, 2026) This package contains the complete raw data, analysis code, and derived outputs needed to reproduce every table, figure, and statistic reported in the paper. The study tests whether agricultural trade disruption can be predicted from country-level and commodity-level production, trade, and climate data across 18 countries and 5 commodities (wheat, rice, maize, soybeans, dairy), 2005–2024, and finds that neither level of prediction outperforms chance once cross-validation is corrected for year-level dependence in the panel — a negative result that also identifies and corrects a cross-validation leakage flaw present in an earlier 13-country version of this analysis. Contents raw_data/ — FAOSTAT production data (QCL domain, downloaded 18 September 2026), two UN Comtrade/ComtradePlus trade-flow exports (HS 0401, 1001, 1005, 1006, 1201; reporter-to-World; 2004–2025), and the World Bank Climate Change Knowledge Portal CRU-TS 4.10 annual temperature and precipitation timeseries (1901–2025). code/ — pipeline.py (panel construction, disruption-event labelling, feature engineering, model definitions, and statistical tests) and run_all.py (the driver script that produces every result in the paper, including a reproduction of the earlier 13-country version under its original rules) and make_figures.py. outputs/ — the assembled 18-country country-commodity-year panel, the commodity-year panel with out-of-fold predictions under both shuffled and leave-one-year-out cross-validation, the 13-country-versus-18-country HHI comparison, the 90-pair vulnerability index with all components, label-permutation null distributions, and a single results.json containing every statistic quoted in the manuscript text. figures/ — all figures as they appear in the paper. Running run_all.py on the raw data regenerates the full results file from scratch (~25 minutes on one CPU core). Software: Python 3.12.3, pandas 3.0.2, scikit-learn 1.8.0, xgboost 3.4.1, numpy 2.4.4, scipy 1.17.1; all random seeds fixed at 42. title: International Congress In Turkey
abstract: Climate change and rural insecurity have become major threats to agricultural production and food security in Nigeria. While climate variability has historically affected farming and pastoral livelihoods, the increasing frequency of droughts, floods, irregular rainfall, rising temperatures and land degradation has intensified pressure on land, water and other productive resources. At the same time, the expansion of armed banditry, particularly across parts of North-Western and North-Central Nigeria, has disrupted farming activities, displaced rural populations, restricted access to agricultural land and weakened local food systems. This paper examines the interconnected relationship between climate change, banditry and food security in Nigeria, focusing on how environmental stress and rural insecurity reinforce agricultural vulnerability. The study adopted a qualitative research design and relied exclusively on secondary data obtained from peer-reviewed journal articles, books, government publications, reports of international organisations, policy documents and credible institutional sources. The data were analysed thematically through documentary analysis. The paper argues that climate change should not be treated as a direct or automatic cause of banditry. Rather, climate-related stress interacts with poverty, competition over land and water, weak governance, insecure land tenure, unemployment, population pressure and the proliferation of small arms to create conditions that may facilitate rural violence and criminality. Banditry subsequently compounds the effects of climate change by forcing farmers away from their fields, destroying agricultural assets, disrupting markets, increasing production and transportation costs and reducing household purchasing power. The resulting decline in agricultural production contributes to food shortages, rising food prices and increased household food insecurity. The paper recommends an integrated policy framework combining climate adaptation, rural security, sustainable land and water management, agricultural investment, early-warning mechanisms, livelihood diversification and stronger local governance. Such an approach is necessary to break the reinforcing cycle between environmental vulnerability, rural insecurity and food insecurity in Nigeria.

title: Brazil Produces 91% of the World's Açaí, 52% of Its Passion Fruit, and 38% of Its Orange Juice. Understanding How It Built That Position Tells You How Global Tropical Fruit Trade Actually Works.
abstract: Brazil Is the Largest Tropical Fruit Producer in the Western Hemisphere and Its Position in Global Trade Reflects Decades of Infrastructure Investment SEO Keywords: Brazil largest tropical fruit producer, Brazil fruit production statistics, Brazil agricultural export history, Brazil fruit infrastructure, Brazil agribusiness development, Brazil Cerrado fruit production Brazil produces more orange juice than any other country on earth. It supplies 91% of the world's commercial açaí, 52% of global passion fruit, and holds sixth position globally for mango production with a rising export trajectory. These figures reflect not just favourable climate and land availability, but a long-term accumulation of irrigation infrastructure, phytosanitary systems, cold chain logistics, and export market development that took four decades to build. The Cerrado biome, spanning central Brazil and covering approximately 200 million hectares, supports large-scale fruit production through a combination of well-drained latosols, reliable rainfall in the growing season, and dry winters that allow controlled flowering and harvest timing. The São Francisco River Valley in northeastern Brazil, where large-scale perimeter irrigation schemes were developed from the 1970s onward, became the country's primary mango and table grape export zone by converting semi-arid land into one of the world's most productive irrigated fruit corridors. Neves and Trombin (2012), reviewing the citrus and tropical fruit supply chains in Brazil in the International Food and Agribusiness Management Review, documented that the Brazilian government's investment in export-oriented irrigation perimeters in the São Francisco Valley between 1975 and 2000 created the physical infrastructure on which private sector investment in packhouses, cold chain, and certification systems was later built, producing a supply chain capable of meeting European Union phytosanitary import requirements (NEVES; TROMBIN, 2012). The São Francisco Valley Turned Semi-Arid Northeastern Brazil Into the Country's Most Productive Export Zone SEO Keywords: São Francisco Valley fruit production, São Francisco Valley mango export, Petrolina Juazeiro fruit, Brazil irrigated mango production, Brazil semi-arid fruit irrigation, Submédio São Francisco horticulture The Submédio São Francisco region, centred on the twin cities of Petrolina (Pernambuco) and Juazeiro (Bahia), produces the majority of Brazil's exported mango and a substantial share of its table grapes. The region receives approximately 400 to 600 millimetres of rainfall annually, which is insufficient for rainfed fruit production, but the São Francisco River provides a perennial water source for the 120,000-hectare public and private irrigation perimeters that were developed from the 1970s through the 1990s under CODEVASF (the São Francisco Valley Development Company). The irrigation infrastructure allowed double-cropping of mango, with farmers able to manipulate flowering through pruning and chemical induction in the dry season to target off-season windows when European and North American market prices are highest. This production calendar advantage, producing mangoes when the Northern Hemisphere is out of season, is the primary commercial logic of the São Francisco Valley's position in global mango trade. FAO (2023), in the FAOSTAT production database, records Brazil's mango production at approximately 1.8 million tonnes annually, with the São Francisco Valley accounting for 70-75% of all fresh mango exports based on regional production data and export documentation (FAO, 2023). Brazilian mangoes, primarily the Tommy Atkins variety developed for shelf life and appearance rather than flavour, reach European supermarkets within 10 to 14 days of harvest through air freight and refrigerated sea freight channels. The fruit, harvested from palm trees in the Amazon floodplain and várzea forests of Pará state, was consumed fresh by Amazonian river communities for centuries. It entered urban Brazilian food culture in the 1990s as a frozen pulp product served in sports nutrition contexts, and then entered international markets in the 2000s as health food trends in North America and Europe created demand for its high anthocyanin content. Brazil produces 91% of global commercial açaí, with Pará state accounting for over 95% of domestic production. The IBGE (2022) municipal agricultural production survey recorded açaí output at approximately 1.2 million tonnes from the state of Pará alone, with farm-gate value growth of over 300% between 2012 and 2022 as international export prices rose with demand (IBGE, 2022). The açaí value chain involves specific logistics not required for other tropical fruits. The fresh fruit degrades within 24 hours of harvest and must be processed into frozen pulp at riverside or municipal processing units within that window. This cold chain requirement has driven investment in small-scale processing infrastructure distributed through the Amazon river system, creating a supply chain model quite different from the large centralized packhouse model of the São Francisco Valley mango trade. title: Comparative Performance of Machine Learning and Deep Learning Algorithms for Agricultural Land Mapping in Anambra State, Nigeria
abstract: Abstract - Accurate delineation of agricultural land is fundamental to agricultural planning, food-security assessment, land-resource management, and monitoring of land-use transformation. However, the heterogeneous and fragmented character of agricultural landscapes in southeastern Nigeria presents substantial challenges for satellite-image classification. This study comparatively evaluated Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Artificial Neural Network (ANN), and Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for agricultural land mapping in Anambra State, Nigeria. Remotely sensed imagery was classified into waterbody, dense forest, agricultural land, built-up area, and bare ground using the four algorithms. Model performance was evaluated using 210 validation samples and multiple confusion-matrix metrics, including sensitivity, precision, specificity, negative predictive value, overall accuracy, balanced accuracy, and Matthew’s correlation coefficient. Agricultural land estimates varied from 1,000.26 km² (21.78%) for SVM to 1,099.12 km² (23.93%) for ANN. SVM achieved the strongest overall performance, recording 88.5% sensitivity, 85.2% precision, 75.0% specificity, 83.3% overall accuracy, 81.7% balanced accuracy, and a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.643. CNN produced the lowest overall accuracy of 74.3%. The findings demonstrate that increased model complexity does not necessarily translate into superior classification performance and establish SVM as an effective approach for regional agricultural land delineation under heterogeneous tropical landscape conditions. Keywords: agricultural land mapping; machine learning; deep learning; Support Vector Machine; Random Forest; artificial neural network; convolutional neural network; remote sensing

title: Strategic Abductive Forecasting (SAF) v1.0: A Unified Probabilistic Framework for Forecasting Systems with Strategic Agents – Compendium of Specification, Theory, Forecasts, and Validation
abstract: This compendium presents the complete specification, mathematical theory, prospective forecasts, and synthetic validation results for Strategic Abductive Forecasting (SAF) v1.0. SAF is a unified hierarchical Bayesian framework that integrates Information Theory (MDL), Bounded-Rationality Game Theory (Quantal Response Equilibrium), and Causal Abductive Inference to forecast complex systems where agents react to each other and to the forecasts themselves (reflexivity). Contents: Part I: Formal Specification: The core generative model, signal extraction filters, and epistemic integrity constraints. Part II: Formal Theory: Mathematical proofs for regret bounds, QRE uniqueness, reflexive fixed points, and anytime-valid misfit detection. Part III: Forecast I (2026–27 El Niño): A prospective forecast of the strategic and socio-economic transmission of the 2026–27 El Niño event, including food prices, export policies, and regional impacts. Part IV: Forecast II (World in 2036): A scenario-based forecast of global demographics, climate, energy, growth, and conflict under deep uncertainty. Part V: Validation (V0): Synthetic recovery tests demonstrating the correctness of the information filter, rationality coefficient recovery, and reflexive iteration. Part VI: Appendices: Full Python source code, raw simulation data, and SHA-256 hashes for reproducibility. Status: SAF v1.0 is a formal specification. The included forecasts (Parts III & IV) are registered prospective forecasts (Level V2) to be scored upon resolution, not validated historical retrodictions. No claim of superior predictive accuracy is made until the full validation protocol (V0–V3) is completed. License: CC-BY-SA 4.0

title: Quantum-Enhanced Anomaly Detection for Supply Chain Disruption Risk in Renewable Energy Component Procurement: An Empirical Comparison of Variational Quantum Circuits and Classical Machine Learning Baselines
abstract: Abstract Renewable energy supply chains — dependent on geographically concentrated raw materials such as lithium, cobalt, rare earths, and polysilicon — are increasingly exposed to procurement disruption risk from geopolitical shocks, commodity price volatility, and demand shifts tied to climate policy. This study develops and empirically tests a hybrid quantum-classical anomaly detection framework using a Variational Quantum Circuit (VQC) to flag early-warning disruption signals in renewable energy procurement data, and benchmarks it against three classical baselines: Isolation Forest, One-Class SVM, and an LSTM Autoencoder. A monthly panel (2008–2025, n = 216) combining the Caldara–Iacoviello Geopolitical Risk Index, World Bank Pink Sheet commodity prices, and IRENA renewable capacity data was engineered into 147 rolling-window features and reduced via PCA to six components for a 6-qubit angle-encoded circuit, implemented independently in PennyLane and Qiskit. Using three documented macro-disruption windows (2008–09 Global Financial Crisis, COVID-19 onset, and the 2022 Russia-Ukraine invasion) as ground truth, the VQC was evaluated against the classical baselines on precision, recall, F1-score, false-positive rate, per-typology recall, noise robustness, and computational cost. Contrary to the study's initial hypotheses, Isolation Forest achieved the highest F1-score (0.593) among all five models, modestly outperforming both VQC implementations (F1 = 0.556). The VQC showed no measurable robustness advantage over Isolation Forest at any tested noise level (0–50% of feature standard deviation) and required approximately 1,230 times longer to train than Isolation Forest for a comparable or weaker result. All models, including the VQC, failed to detect the COVID-19-era logistics disruption window. These findings suggest that, on this dataset and circuit design, near-term quantum machine learning does not yet offer a measurable advantage over well-tuned classical anomaly detectors for renewable energy procurement risk monitoring, and the paper discusses the practical and methodological implications of this null result for procurement risk management and future QML research.

title: FOOD INFLATION IN INDIA: MYTH OR REALITY
abstract: The acceleration in food inflation and the abnormally high level of food prices have been caused by several factors relating to a shock in supply, trade, global prices, food manage­ment, speculative activities and demand. Some of these factors are of a short-term nature and some are of a long-term nature, while some operate both in the short as well as long period. Long-term inflation depends upon the pace of growth in domestic production in relation to the growth in demand. This involves three aspects: Level or magni­tude of growth of output, Year to year fluctuations, and Composition of growth. Changes in international prices are exert­ing a significant direct and indirect influ­ence on domestic food prices through trade as well as through adjustment in domestic policies in order to keep some balance with global prices. There is a need to change regulation in food markets to encourage and involve the private sector in the food market, trade and stock management for price stabilization along with active participation of public agencies. The risk of such players resorting to hoarding and speculative trade can be checked by establishing a Food Market Regulator. India also needs to set up a strong institutional mechanism for an early warning system relating to food demand, supply and price situation. The long-run food scenario is causing greater concern as growth in food output is decelerating. The dependence on productivity for food growth is rising, which, in turn, involves an increase in the average cost of production. This implies that growth in food output is driven by an increase in food prices. To keep food inflation at a low level, there is a need to take strong action to develop and disseminate improved technologies for raising food production.

title: Fertilizer Use and Maize output in Sub-Saharan Africa: Empirical Evidence from Selected African Countries
abstract: Fertilizer consumption in Sub-Saharan Africa countries has been found to remain low as compared to countries in similar level in other parts of the world. This has led to stagnation and declined yields in most crops across parts of Sub-Saharan Africa for several decades while that in countries that have increased fertilizer use have seen their agricultural productivity considerably increased over the years. This paper examines the effect of fertilizer use on maize output in selected African countries for the period 1990-2010 using data on fertilizer application rates. The data was analyzed using fixed effects regression based on a Cobb-Douglas production function. To take care of country differences in terms of production environments, country dummies were used in the fixed effects estimation. Empirical results indicated that maize output was positively and significantly correlated with land, labour, rainfall, aggregate fertilizer use, nitrogen and phosphorous nutrient fertilizers with land and labour having the highest effect on maize output in Sub-Saharan Africa To take care of rainfall vulnerabilities that could easily negate the positive effect of rainfall, supplementary irrigation measures should be put in place which could include rain water harvesting and small-scale water storage among maize producing households. Given the indication that fertilizer use was low despite its positive influence in maize output, it is recommended that strategies be put in place by relevant stakeholders in respective countries in a bid to boost aggregate and nutrient fertilizer use so as to further increase maize output and these could include price reduction strategies like subsidies and timely availability of fertilizer, reduction in import fee, clearance and warehouse charges at the ports of entry as a way of reducing the final market price. It could also be necessary for creation of more awareness among maize producers on the importance of adequate fertilizer use especially through agricultural extension workers and other relevant stakeholders.

title: Harnessing the potentials of millet production for food defense and economic diversification in Nigeria
abstract: Time series data that spanned from 1961 to 2018 sourced from FAO database, covering production, area and yield were used to examine the food security trend of millet production in Nigeria. The collected data were analyzed using both descriptive and inferential statistics. The findings showed poor performance in the production of millet as growth was driven by area other than productivity. It was observed that price volatility triggered high fluctuation in area and yield, thus causing high instability in the production of millet. In addition, production risk and uncertainty were the major sources of production variability between the regime shifts. It was observed that a surge in the average production level between regime shifts owed majorly to area expansion. The empirical evidence showed that the farmers’ decision on current acreage allocation for millet was governed by both institutional and non-institution factors. Furthermore, the forecast showed that the country will be faced with millet food insecurity to battle with; as critical reliance on millet importation will expose the country to risks from global food price spikes and shortages; and geopolitical and environmental threats. Therefore, the study recommends the need for long-term domestic self-sufficiency in millet production capable of feeding the country’s population as a key strategic food goal.

title: ARMA BASED CROP YIELD PREDICTION USING TEMPERATURE AND RAINFALL PARAMETERS WITH GROUND WATER LEVEL CLASSIFICATION
abstract: Nowadays, wireless telecommunication networks are promising alternative for rainfall measuring instruments that complement previous monitoring devices. Due to big dataset of the rainfall and the telecommunication networks data, empirical computational methods represnt less adequate of actual data. So, deep learning models are proposed for the analysis of big data and give more accurate presentation of real measurements. This project investigated rainfall monitoring results from experimental measurements. The main aim of this study is to provide a methodology for rainfall data classification based on neural network methods based on the historical rainfall data production data. Classification based on the previous years of rainfall can help farmers take necessary steps to measure crop production in the coming season. Understanding and assessing future crop production can help ensure food security and reduce impacts of climate change. In this work, ARMA (Auto Regressive Moving Average) method is used for proposed work. Past ten years of data set is taken for rainfall and ground water level for our country. The proposed work classifies the ground water level data set records using ARIMA model to predict the model for future test record data sets. title: Soil Erosion on United States. Present and Future (2020-2050)
abstract: Brought on by anthropogenic actions, accelerated soil erosion inflicts extreme changes in terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems. These field-scale (30 m) changes have neither been fully surveyed in the present, nor predicted for a probable future. Water-driven soil erosion (i.e., sheet and rill erosion) rates across the contiguous United States were estimated for the present, and then predicted for the future using three alternative Shared Socioeconomic Pathway and Representative Concentration Pathway (SSP-RCP) scenarios (2.6, 4.5, and 8.5) of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6). The G2 erosion model which is integrated with Machine Learning (ML) and Remote Sensing (RS) techniques were used to estimate soil erosion based on gauge observations of long-term precipitation, and climate and land use land cover (LULC) scenarios. The baseline model (2020) estimated soil erosion rates of 2.32 Mg ha−1 yr−1 under current conservation agriculture practices (CPs). Maintaining current CPs, future scenarios predict an 8 % to 21 % increase in soil erosion under different combinations of SSP-RCP climate and LULC change scenarios. The findings of this study can help policy makers for future conservation planning on maintaining soil fertility, mitigating environmental impacts, and promoting food security. This reprository provide the soil erosion maps for united states in present and future.

title: FPCA - From mobile app-based crowdsourcing to crowd-trusted food price estimates in Nigeria: pre-processing and post-sampling strategy for optimal statistical inference
abstract: Timely and reliable monitoring of commodity food prices is an essential requirement for the assessment of market and food security risks and the establishment of early warning systems, especially in developing economies. However, data from regional or national systems for tracking changes of food prices in sub-Saharan Africa lacks the temporal or spatial richness and is often insufficient to inform targeted interventions. In addition to limited opportunity for [near-]real-time assessment of food prices, various stages in the commodity supply chain are mostly unrepresented, thereby limiting insights on stage-related price evolution. Yet, governments and market stakeholders rely on commodity price data to make decisions on appropriate interventions or commodity-focused investments. Recent rapid technological development indicates that digital devices and connectivity services are becoming affordable for many, including in remote areas of developing economies. This offers a great opportunity both for the harvesting of price data (via new data collection methodologies, such as crowdsourcing/crowdsensing — i.e. citizen-generated data — using mobile apps/devices), and for disseminating it (via web dashboards or other means) to provide real-time data that can support decisions at various levels and related policy-making processes. However, market information that aims at improving the functioning of markets and supply chains requires a continuous data flow as well as quality, accessibility and trust. More data does not necessarily translate into better information. Citizen-based data-generation systems are often confronted by challenges related to data quality and citizen participation, which may be further complicated by the volume of data generated compared to traditional approaches. Following the food price hikes during the first noughties of the 21st century, the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC) started working on innovative methodologies for real-time food price data collection and analysis in developing countries. The work carried out so far includes a pilot initiative to crowdsource data from selected markets across several African countries, two workshops (with relevant stakeholders and experts), and the development of a spatial statistical quality methodology to facilitate the best possible exploitation of geo-located data. Based on the latter, the JRC designed the Food Price Crowdsourcing Africa (FPCA) project and implemented it within two states in Northern Nigeria. The FPCA is a credible methodology, based on the voluntary provision of data by a crowd (people living in urban, suburban, and rural areas) using a mobile app, leveraging monetary and non-monetary incentives to enhance contribution, which makes it possible to collect, analyse and validate, and disseminate staple food price data in real time across market segments. The granularity and high frequency of the crowdsourcing data open the door to real-time space-time analysis, which can be essential for policy and decision making and rapid response on specific geographic regions. title: COMPARITIVE STUDY OF ARIMA AND ANN FOR TIME SERIES PREDICTION OF BLACKGRAM PRICES OF ANDHRA PRADESH
abstract: Food price predictions are meant to be helpful for farmers, decision-makers, and the agribusiness sectors.So as to plan the crops, imports, exports and for storage.This study aimed to provide insight into the problem of Blackgram pulse price volatility modelling in Andhra Pradesh.Data on prices of black gram collected over a period of 22 years (1991 January to 2022 September) from Agricultural Market Intelligence center, Lam, Guntur.The high volatility in Black gram prices had mainly due to supply and demand shocks.In order to determine the best model to capture the trend of Blackgram prices, a comparison study between the Auto Regressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA) and Artificial Neural Network models (ANN) were studied.The model selection criterion for this study were Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE).The Ljung-Box test was also tried to verify the adequacy of the selected model.Finally, NNAR (8-9-1) model was found as most appropriate to capture the trend of Blackgram prices of Andhra Pradesh, and the forecasts were estimated.The prices of Blackgram ranges between Rs. 6982 and Rs.7116 for next 12 months.The R software had been used for analysing the data.

title: Modelling the Spread of PCN in Scotland
abstract: Potato cyst nematodes (PCN) cost Scottish agriculture over £25 million/year and threatens food security in the developed and developing world. Improved understanding of PCN epidemiology is a priority for the Scottish potato industry, with spatial and temporal modelling identified by the recent PHC PCN working group as essential components. The aim of this project was to gain a better understanding of the spatial epidemiology of PCN in Scotland, by applying mapping, statistical and artificial intelligence (machine learning) techniques to existing landscape-scale datasets. Several factors were shown to influence the presence of PCN in fields, either positively or negatively, which may help to better understand how management practices could be used to help reduce the presence of the pest. These principal drivers of PCN incidence were used to create a machine learning model that can predict PCN incidence to an accuracy of 82%.

title: Exploration of Illegal, Unreported, Unregulated Fishing and Vessel Relationships using AIS Data and Machine Learning
abstract: Illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing is a key driver of global overfishing, threatens marine ecosystems, puts food security and regional stability at risk, and is linked to major human rights violations and even organized crime [8]. The ability to predict both where and when IUU fishing is likely occurring provides significant advantages to coast guards with limited resources. In this paper, we provide three resources to aid in the ability to identify IUU fishing. First, we created an algorithm to identify refrigeration ships that often meet with fishing vessels to transport the catch to port. Next, we explored the relationships between these vessels and ports. To do so, we displayed not only the traffic coming and going, but also the statistics surrounding the vessels next visited port via an interactive dashboard. Lastly, we explored an Item Response Theory (IRT) Model that bears a relationship between variables obtained from the fishing vessels’ AIS communication and probability that IUU fishing activity is occurring. We also created and used a Density Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) model to explore areas where IUU fishing occurs most often. We approached the problem as an exploratory data problem, with the primary objective of understanding the significance of certain parameters, models, or instances of IUU activity in the data as an initial point of reference for future work.

title: H2020 DeepCube UC2: Climate Induced Migration in Africa Public Datacube
abstract: This is the public datacube for UC2 climate induced migration in Africa (2015-2023) The input data includes varied data sources, environmental and climatic variables from Earth Observation data and relevant socioeconomic data sources accounting for the main drivers of drought displacement in Somalia. The Earth Observation data cube includes variables from ERA5 Land such as 2m Temperature, Potential Evaporation, Total Precipitation and the Volumetric soil water layers, the ESA CCI land cover map and the precipitation dataset captured from Climate Hazards Center InfraRed Precipitation with Station data (CHIRPS). The precipitation data from CHIRPS and the Potential Evaporation from ERA5 are used to compute the Standardized Precipitation and Evaporation Index (SPEI) that is a robust indicator for drought conditions accounting for both precipitation and temperature extremes. Regarding socioeconomic sources, the food security dimension is represented by market prices variables in different local markets like the price of livestock (for instance, Cattle, Camel, etc.) and harvest products (e.g., wheat, rice, maize, etc.). We also include the violent conflict data captured from the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED) given the close link existing between droughts and conflict in Somalia. Finally, the dataset of Internal Displacement Somalia is obtained via the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) Protection & Return Monitoring Network (PRMN).

title: Crop Yield and Price Prediction
abstract: Crop yield and price detection are crucial factors in agriculture that affect farmers' income and food production. Machine learning techniques have been increasingly used to predict crop yield and price based on various parameters such as environmental, soil, and crop features. This study proposes a combined approach of using random forest for price detection and decision tree regression for crop yield detection. The model is trained and tested on a large dataset of crop parameters and historical prices. Results indicate that the proposed model outperforms existing methods with an accuracy of 88.5% for price detection and 89.2% for crop yield detection. The model's ability to accurately predict crop yield and price can assist farmers and policymakers in making informed decisions about crop production and marketing, ultimately improving food security and agricultural sustainability.

title: A new proposal for forecasting inflation in the eurozone: a global model
abstract: This paper evaluates the forecasting performance of the relatively new machine learning Global Unrefined (GlobalUN, hereafter) model with respect to inflation in the Eurozone. In this global pooled neural network framework, we use a quarterly panel dataset covering 20 euro-area countries (2001Q1–2025Q1) together with the EA-20 aggregate, which includes key variables such as HICP, energy prices, food, and others. Thus, the network remains simple yet flexible enough to absorb heterogeneity across countries. Our contribution of our work is crucial since monetary policy in the Eurozone hinges on accurate inflation forecasts (i.e., as ECB decisions target expected rather than current inflation). Our findings are crystal clear. The GlobalUn model outperforms all other benchmark models and the advanced machine learning XGBoost model in almost all Eurozone countries and horizons (i.e., the NAÏVE model seems to outperform in a few cases). These results are useful for policymakers, central banks, and fiscal institutions, as they should take the GlobalUN model into account as part of their arsenal.

title: An Artificial Intelligence Framework for Food Supply Chain Management: Policy Implications for UAE Public-Sector Agricultural Authorities
abstract: Artificial intelligence offers significant potential to strengthen food supply chain management in countries facing resource constraints and food security pressures. This study develops and empirically evaluates an AI framework within the Abu Dhabi Agriculture and Food Safety Authority and derives policy implications for UAE public-sector agricultural authorities. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was administered to operational employees. Of 500 questionnaires distributed from a population of 1,506 employees, 402 valid responses were retained after data screening. The data were analysed using SPSS and Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling. The model examined four AI capabilities, namely Expert System, Machine Learning, Agent-Based System, and Artificial Neural Network, in relation to three food supply chain outcomes: Production and Sourcing, Logistics and Distribution Efficiency, and Safety and Quality Control. Six of the twelve hypothesized relationships were supported. Artificial Neural Network was significantly associated with all three outcomes, Expert System with Production and Sourcing and Safety and Quality Control, and Agent-Based System with Logistics and Distribution Efficiency. Machine Learning showed no significant direct effects. Although the structural model demonstrated predictive relevance, several constructs recorded average variance extracted values below 0.50; therefore, the findings should be interpreted with caution. The study proposes a capability-based policy framework emphasizing AI governance, data infrastructure, workforce readiness, institutional coordination, and phased implementation. Sustainability is treated as a broader policy objective supported through improved operational resilience, efficiency, and safety rather than as a directly measured outcome.

title: Climate Risk Perception and Behavioural Biases in Real Estate Investment Markets: A Systematic Review
abstract: Climate Change poses increasing physical and transitional risks to real estate markets, yetinvestment decisions continue to show systematic misperception of these hazards. This review synthesises recent empirical and theoretical literature on climate risk perception and behavioural biases in real estate investment markets, focusing on Ghana andcomparative African economies. Following the PRISMA 2020 Protocol and based on over 2500 records identified from Scopus and Web of Science, 30 peer-reviewed studies between 2020 and 2025 were selected after screening and synthesised to address four research questions regarding how real estate investors perceive climate risk, what behavioural variables mediate their responses, whether market prices reflect these perceptions, and which theoretical lenses best explain observed behaviours. Three key findings emerged. One, climate risk perception is consistently distorted by cognitive biases, including availability heuristics, loss aversion, optimism bias, and herding. Two, climate risks are being capitalised into property prices, with flood-risk discounts of 12-18% documented in Accra and 6-15% in U.S. coastal markets. However, pricing remains reactive, incomplete and highly unequal across geographies. Three, developer adaptation is driven primarily by financial incentives and regulatory pressure rather than proactive, forward-looking risk management. Grounded in Prospect Theory (Kahneman, 1979) and the Adaptive Market Hypothesis (Lo, 2004), the review attributes these patterns to a structural market failure. The study recommends that policymakers in Ghana and comparable African economies prioritise investment in standardised, publicly accessible climate hazard data and mandatory climate risk disclosure frameworks as a foundational step towards closing the perception-reality gap in real estate climate risk pricingand fostering more resilient, climate-adaptive property markets

title: Comparison of Premium Rice Price Prediction in East Java with ARIMA and LSTM (Case Study: National Food Agency Data)
abstract: Rice price prediction plays a crucial role in maintaining economic stability and food security, especially in East Java, one of Indonesia's major rice production centers. This study aims to forecast premium rice prices in East Java using the ARIMA (AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average) method. The data utilized in this research comprises premium rice prices obtained from the National Food Agency over the period from March 15, 2021, to October 17, 2024. The analysis process begins with data exploration to identify trends and seasonal patterns in the rice price data. Subsequently, the data is analyzed using ARIMA and LSTM methods, both recognized for their effectiveness in time-series forecasting. The ARIMA(1,1,1) model was selected due to its capability to capture price dynamics through its autoregressive, integrated, and moving average components, making it well-suited for linear data with minimal seasonal variation. LSTM was employed as a comparative model because it is a subset of Machine Learning that integrates computational models and neural network algorithms, offering potential improvements in prediction accuracy. The LSTM model used for prediction consists of four layers, each with 50 neurons, dropout rates of 20% and 30%, and a single output layer representing the predicted price. The results indicate the ARIMA model provides highly accurate price estimates with a Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 0.485%, whereas the LSTM model achieves a MAPE of 1.95%. These findings serve as a reference for policymakers and food industry stakeholders in formulating strategic measures to stabilize rice prices in East Java.

title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in U.S. Agriculture: A Review: Assessing advancements, challenges, and the potential impact on food production and sustainability
abstract: This study systematically reviews the transformative role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in enhancing agricultural productivity and sustainability in the United States. With the aim of understanding how AI technologies can be effectively integrated into farming practices, this research employs a systematic literature review methodology, focusing on peer-reviewed journal articles, conference proceedings, and reputable reports from 2010 to 2024. The methodology includes a structured search strategy, defined inclusion and exclusion criteria, and thematic analysis to categorize findings into relevant themes. Key findings reveal that AI technologies, such as machine learning models, predictive analytics, and robotics, are revolutionizing U.S. agriculture by optimizing resource use, improving crop health monitoring, and enhancing decision-making processes. Despite the promising potential of AI to address challenges like food security and environmental sustainability, the adoption of AI in agriculture faces barriers including technological adoption, data privacy concerns, and the need for significant investment in digital infrastructure. The study concludes that leveraging AI for sustainable agriculture requires collaborative efforts among stakeholders, including investment in digital literacy, development of regulatory frameworks, and fostering public-private partnerships. Future research directions emphasize the socio-economic impacts of AI adoption, ethical considerations, and the development of scalable AI solutions. This study underscores AI's pivotal role in ensuring a sustainable, productive, and resilient agricultural sector.

title: The Fed as a Moral Enterprise
abstract: At two o'clock in the afternoon of the final meeting day of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) of the Federal Reserve, one will find tens of thousands of traders and investment managers glued to their computer screens, waiting for the moment when a two-hundred- to three-hundred-word summary of the meeting will be published. Every word will be parsed for special meaning. For these professionals a lot is riding on the outcome. The stock and bond markets are likely to react one way if the tone of the statement is “hawkish” and implies a tightening of money supply and credit terms, and in another if the decision is “dovish” or accommodative, suggesting monetary and credit easing. The dovish statements benefit certain types of asset classes and groups of investors, the hawkish others. This two-hundred-word FOMC statement can and often does move markets by hundreds of billions and even trillions of dollars. Winners—the traders and managers whose actions appropriately anticipated the direction of the FOMC—stand to benefit enormously, while losers go down in defeat.1However, what is going on in these FOMC meetings involves far more than determining market winners and losers. The FOMC statement has a bearing on almost every aspect of commercial and private life. And yet, very few people outside the professionals mentioned above realize what is at stake; most don't know what the FOMC is or what the Federal Reserve actually does, and have only a vague sense about issues of interest rate and banking policy. For better or worse, the discussion of such matters is for the most part now mostly left to those who claim special expertise in macroeconomic theory.Volumes have been written about the technical issues and the nuances of the Federal Reserve System and the FOMC monetary policy-making responsibility. I want to pay some attention to that analysis, as it provides the foundation required for even a rudimentary assessment of these entities. However, my interests ultimately move in another direction. I want to show that the making of U.S. monetary policy is inescapably a moral enterprise; thus an analysis of its implicit moral presumptions provides an important mode of evaluation of the FOMC decisions and the policy actions taken.Without making the whole case here, I will argue that monetary policy making is a moral enterprise first off because it inherently involves distributional consequences, which by their very nature demand an accounting based on fairness and justice. Monetary policy involves moral issues at even a more fundamental level as the responsibility for the currency is bound up in duties and obligations associated with the social contract—duties that have to do with honoring contractarian promises. While couched in economic terms like “currency debasement” or “debt monetization,” criticisms here actually represent a moral charge that government promises are not being kept.
