title: Impact of Intelligent Agriculture on Sustainability and Food Security
abstract: Agricultural systems face increasing challenges related to resource depletion, climate variability, and food insecurity, requiring innovative and sustainable solutions. This study examines the impact of intelligent agriculture on sustainability performance and food security outcomes. A quantitative comparative design was employed, involving several farms categorized into intelligent agriculture adopters and conventional farmers. Data were analyzed using a sliding time-window approach, Structural Equation Modeling (SEM), and predictive machine learning techniques to evaluate direct and mediated effects. The findings reveal that intelligent agriculture significantly improves yield (33% increase), reduces water and fertilizer use (approximately 25%), and decreases production variability by more than 50%. Sustainability performance strongly mediates the relationship between intelligent agriculture and food security, resulting in a 27% improvement in the Food Security Index. These results confirm that intelligent agriculture enhances long-term agricultural resilience and resource efficiency, providing empirical support for policies promoting digital farming technologies to achieve sustainable food systems.

title: MACHINE LEARNING-BASED APPROACHES TO IMPROVE CROP YIELD PREDICTION IN AGRICULTURE IN ADAMAWA STATE, NIGERIA
abstract: Accurate yield forecasting is critical for sustainable agriculture in developing countries like Nigeria. This study evaluates three machine learning models: Artificial Neural Network (ANN), Decision Tree (DT), and Support Vector Machine (SVM) for predicting crop yields across five agriculturally diverse Local Government Areas in Adamawa State, Nigeria. Using environmental data from 2019 to 2023, including rainfall, temperature, and soil moisture, we trained models to forecast yields (kg/ha) for staple crops like maize, sorghum, and groundnuts. Results showed that ANN and DT outperformed SVM, achieving high accuracy (R²: 0.93–0.98) and low errors (RMSE: 5.5–10.9). While the ANN excelled in Madagali (R²=0.97, RMSE=6.7), the DT performed best in Mubi North (R²=0.98, RMSE=5.5), whereas the SVM consistently underperformed (R²: 0.42–0.46; RMSE: 29.8–36.6) in all study areas. The result also showed rainfall and soil moisture were stronger yield predictors than temperature. These results demonstrate ANN and DT’s suitability for yield prediction in diverse environments. We recommend that models which prioritize rainfall and soil moisture over temperature be employed in crop yield prediction in the study areas and ANN or DT tools are to be adopted to aid smallholder farmers in farm resource planning. These will reduce prediction errors by 76 to 82% compared to traditional methods, enabling proactive resource allocation and enhancing food security in Northern Nigeria.

title: CLIMATE MITIGATION AND DEVELOPMENT TRADE-OFFS IN THE GLOBAL SOUTH: REASSESSING POVERTY, HUNGER, AND EQUITY IN GLOBAL CLIMATE GOVERNANCE
abstract: Climate change mitigation is an urgent global priority, but its pursuit poses disproportionate challenges for developing countries that contribute minimally to global emissions yet bear the brunt of climate impacts. These countries also face immediate developmental needs, including poverty reduction, food security, healthcare, and education, creating tensions between addressing urgent socio-economic concerns and implementing long-term mitigation strategies. The central puzzle of this research is “should climate change mitigation be a priority for developing countries, given the more immediate concerns of reducing poverty and hunger for today’s generation? This study hence, examines whether climate change mitigation should be prioritized by developing countries, with a focus on the energy and agricultural sectors that are both major emitting sectors yet critical for livelihoods. Drawing on case study insights from Nigeria and Nepal, this research analyzes trade-offs, co-benefits, and synergies of climate policies, employing climate justice and sustainable development theories. This study argues that while mitigation is important, it must not overshadow urgent developmental needs; instead, a balanced, equity-driven, and context-specific approach is required, supported by financial and technological transfers from wealthier nations. Findings reveal that mitigation policies, if implemented without progressive redistribution, risk deepening poverty, increasing food prices, and exacerbating inequalities, particularly in Sub-Saharan Africa. However, evidence also suggests that integrated approaches such as sustainable agriculture, renewable energy expansion, international financial transfers, and just transition frameworks, can create co-benefits that simultaneously advance development and climate goals. The study concludes that developing countries require spatial time, financial and technological support, and equity-centered global climate governance to harmonize poverty alleviation with climate action. Finally, a balanced approach that addresses urgent developmental needs while gradually advancing mitigation is essential for sustainable and just global futures.

title: APPLICATION OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN SOIL FERTILITY ASSESSMENT AND CROP YIELD PREDICTION IN SOUTHWEST NIGERIA: A STATISTICAL APPROACH
abstract: This study investigates the application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques in soil fertility assessment and crop yield prediction in Southwest Nigeria. Traditional soil analysis methods are often time-consuming, expensive, and limited in predictive capability. This research integrates machine learning models to analyse soil parameters such as pH, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and organic matter content to predict crop yield outcomes. Data were obtained from selected agricultural zones in Osun and Oyo States. Supervised learning algorithms including Linear Regression, Random Forest, and Support Vector Machines were employed. The results indicate that AI-based models significantly improve prediction accuracy compared to conventional statistical approaches, with Random Forest outperforming other models. The study demonstrates that AI can enhance decision-making in precision agriculture, optimize fertilizer application, and improve food security. It is recommended that stakeholders adopt AI-driven soil analysis systems to boost agricultural productivity in Nigeria.

title: Predictive AI Models for Food Spoilage and Shelf-Life Estimation
abstract: Food spoilage is a global problem which causes food waste, economic loss and foodborne illness. The shelf life and spoilage estimation of food is traditionally done with fixed expiration dates and this leads to disposal of still eatable food or eating spoiled food. Recently, with the development of the Artificial Intelligence (AI), the predictive models have been developed to better evaluate the food spoilage based on such factors as temperature, humidity, microbial activities and gas emissions. This paper discusses the part played by AI in the prediction of food spoilage, while also outlining various machine learning and deep learning models (regression, classification, convolutional neural network – CNN and hybrid AI). Food spoilage estimation powered by AI relies on multiple sources of data including IoT enabled sensors, Spectroscopy as well as real time environmental monitoring. The practical use in the food industry of such data driven models is in the context of real life applications as smart packaging, AI powered quality in supply chains, retail inventory product optimization. However, the adoption of AI in this field is limited as the data is scarce and of low quality, the models have limited accuracy, ethical concerns exist, and implementation is expensive. In this review, potential for AI in transforming food spoilage estimation is highlighted and this could be achieved by working on obtaining greater accuracy, scalability, and adoption of the model in different food sectors. The role of AI in enhancing food security, sustainability and efficient use of resources, waste reduction and increasing accessibility of good quality perishables to every consumer will gain increasing feasibility with the improvement in AI.

title: Enhancements in Agricultural Forecasting in Bundelkhand Facilitated by the Use of Artificial Intelligence
abstract: The Bundelkhand region comprises more than fifty percent of Uttar Pradesh's total pulse farming area, although its output is inferior to the state average. This requires the execution of many technical interventions, alongside the establishment of infrastructure as well as marketing tactics. Developing sophisticated predictive models is crucial for properly forecasting crop yields, as changes in the climate and rising unpredictability intensify the worldwide food safety dilemma. A sophisticated prediction model for projecting crop yields was created to tackle these difficulties. The model aimed to address concerns about global food security in light of the increasing population. The study focuses on eleven widely farmed crops in Bundelkhand. The Bundelkhand area produces crops like cassava, maize, potatoes, rice (paddy), soybeans, and wheat. Groundnut, cotton, mustard, and cotton. The integration of Artificial Neural Networks, or ANN, alongside the Optimization Algorithm resulted in the development of an artificial intelligence system designed to accomplish this goal. The model integrates meteorological conditions, pesticide use, and historical yield data.After training the ANN with an improved model using 70 percent of the data that was accessible, we assessed its performance with the final thirty percent. A comparison was performed between the model's accuracy and that of ANN models, using statistical benchmarks. The suggested model surpassed other models, attaining superior measurements with an RMSE of 14.83, MAE of 88.53, MAPE of 0.07, and a R² of 0.98 overall agricultural production prediction. The results demonstrate an improvement in the accuracy and reliability of agricultural output forecasts compared to the currently used methods. A comprehensive system aimed at augmenting agricultural production forecasting via enhanced predictive skills, hence possibly improving the effectiveness of resources and optimizing crop management, is shown by the proposed model. This study illustrates the capacity of machine learning to tackle global agricultural issues and improve food security measures, holding substantial importance for agricultural strategy and formulation of policies.

title: Fisheries and Aquatic Animal Health: Diseases, Aquaculture, Biosecurity, and Sustainability
abstract: Aquaculture represents one of the fastest-growing food production industries in the world, supporting fish, shrimp and shellfish production, as well as seaweed for the human edible food chain and livelihoods in Asia, Africa and Latin America. But along with this increase, ever present is the threat of aquatic animal disease. White spot syndrome virus, tilapia lake virus, and “vibriosis” can wipe out an entire crop in days, jeopardizing food security, export markets and rural livelihoods. Traditional fish health management, which rely on farmer experience, visual inspections, and laboratory diagnosis, are useful but still have some drawbacks such as time intensive, difficult to scale and expensive. This book addresses this void by focusing on artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, and deep learning in the centre of aquatic animal health. It demonstrates through seven chapters how such data-driven tools are transforming disease detection, risk prediction and decision-making for sustainable aquaculture. Chapter 1 comprises an introduction to artificial intelligence and machine learning for disease detection, computer vision and behaviour monitoring. Multi-omics, microbiome science, and systems biology are discussed, including genomics, metabolomics and digital twins, in Chapter 2. Chapter 3 reviews environmental DNA (eDNA), metagenomics and molecular epidemiology for aquatic disease surveillance. Chapter 4 discusses antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in a One Health perspective. In Chapter 5, factors related to climate change and the emergence of diseases are discussed with an emphasis on aquaculture health management strategies that are inclusive of climate resilience. Chapter 6 focuses on developing predictive biosecurity and outbreak forecasting for data-driven disease prevention. Finally, chapter 7 covers precision aquaculture and digital health, including the Internet of Things (IoT), biosensors, edge computing and real-time monitoring. The subjects of these chapters can be summarised under three themes. One is integration: Animal health cannot be achieved with the help of any single sensor, assay or algorithm – rather, big data from water quality sensors, imaging, genome surveillance and farm records need to be aggregated in new early warning systems. The second is sustainability: smarter health management reduces death, feed waste and antibiotic use, for food security, animal welfare and environmental protection. The third one is responsible innovation. Each chapter tackles the complex issues of data quality, model validation, explainable AI, regulation, and fair access – especially for small-scale seafood farmers, who generate a significant share of the seafood harvested globally. In all cases practical impact is emphasized. Worked perspectives on image-based diagnostics of disease, acoustics and feeding behaviour, water quality forecasting, pathogen genomics and risk modelling are all presented and relate to the realities of costs, infrastructure and skills on the actual farm. The book is intended for a wide audience such as students and researchers, aquatic veterinarians, fish health specialists, fish farmers, extension officers, technology upgrades and policymakers in related fields. Technical ideas are presented in accessible terms, with figures, overview tables and hands-on suggestions, allowing readers from various disciplines, such as biology, data science and engineering, to glean from others. We hope that this volume will provide a foundation and guide the way for scientists and technologists dedicated to the development of resilient, evidence-based, and technology-enabled aquaculture.

title: Publishing academic books in emerging fields: Strategies for success and overcoming challenges
abstract: Publishing academic books in emerging fields presents unique opportunities and challenges in today's dynamic scholarly landscape. Academic publishers and authors must navigate a rapidly changing ecosystem shaped by technological advances, market demands, and interdisciplinary collaboration as new research areas emerge. This paper discusses how to publish academic books in cutting-edge fields despite the challenges. Monitoring academic journals, conferences, and research networks helps identify trends early. First-mover advantages are available to authors and publishers in emerging fields. However, rigorous academic standards and flexibility to adapt to unconventional topics and methods must be balanced. Academic publishing is being transformed by digital tools like artificial intelligence, which improve manuscript preparation, peer review, and niche audience marketing. Innovation is needed to overcome initial readership, established scholar skepticism, and a lack of comprehensive frameworks for under-researched areas. To overcome these barriers, open access publishing and collaborations with research institutions and funding bodies are essential. Multimedia content like interactive e-books and augmented reality apps offers new ways to teach. This chapter uses successful case studies, industry reports, and leading academic publishers' insights. Synthesizing these perspectives gives authors and publishers a roadmap to succeed in emerging fields and make their contributions impactful, credible, and widely accessible in the digital age. The chapter emphasizes academic publishing's transformative power to advance knowledge and innovation. Keywords: Book publishing, Book publishers, ISBN, Publish monographs, Low-cost publishing, Google scholar, Open access books. Citation: Rane, N. L., Choudhary, S., & Rane, J. (2024). Publishing academic books in emerging fields: Strategies for success and overcoming challenges. In How to Publish Academic Books: A Guide to Publishing Monographs, Edited Volumes, Textbooks, and Theses (pp. 145-189). Deep Science Publishing. https://doi.org/10.70593/978-81-982935-8-9_4 4.1 Introduction Technological advances, research paradigm shifts, and interdisciplinary scholarship are changing academic book publishing at an unprecedented rate (Coser et al., 1982; Tian & Martin, 2010; Weedon, 2017). Academic books provide comprehensive information and in-depth analysis to researchers and practitioners in emerging fields, where knowledge boundaries are constantly being redefined. Publishing in these new domains presents unique challenges and opportunities that require a strategic approach to succeed. Emerging fields often cross disciplines, requiring new methods and diverse perspectives. Due to societal and global needs, artificial intelligence ethics, climate-resilient technologies, quantum computing, and digital humanities are rising (Baverstock & Bowen, 2019; Engels et al., 2018; Rane et al., 2024a). Academic publishers must find, curate, and distribute high-quality content that meets scholarly and market needs as these researchers explore new territory. Open-access publishing and digital platforms have transformed academic publishing, emphasizing accessibility, visibility, and impact. Authors must now balance scholarly rigor with the ability to engage diverse audiences and use modern dissemination tools to succeed. Unpredictability is a major issue when publishing academic books in emerging fields (Canoy et al., 2006; Adema & Schmidt, 2010; Steele, 2008; Meti & Malipatil, 2024). Emerging fields have little foundational literature, making it hard to predict their long-term relevance and readership. In a fast-changing intellectual environment, authors and publishers must balance timely publication with obsolescence to keep their works relevant (Harzing, 2010; Ross & Collier, 2010; Clark & Phillips, 2019; Patil et al., 2024a). Traditional academic gatekeepers may struggle to assess the relevance and quality of interdisciplinary research. New peer review and editorial methods that prioritize inclusivity and adaptability are needed. Academic book publishing faces new opportunities and challenges due to digital transformation. E-books, digital repositories, and platforms like Amazon Kindle Direct Publishing and IngramSpark have democratized publishing tools, allowing scholars from diverse backgrounds to publish. The ease of self-publishing has raised quality control concerns, forcing authors and publishers to emphasize rigorous editorial standards and ethical practices. Advanced analytics and data-driven marketing strategies are essential for targeting audiences, optimizing discoverability, and promoting academic books in emerging fields. Understanding and using these tools helps authors increase their impact. Funding is crucial in academic book publishing, especially in emerging fields without institutional or commercial support (Greco, 2013; Giménez-Toledo et al., 2017; Patil et al., 2024b; Rane et al., 2024b). Research councils, foundations, and academic societies help fund high-quality production, peer review, and open-access dissemination. Collaborations between academia, industry, and publishing houses are becoming more important in connecting academic knowledge to practical applications. These partnerships make academic books more relevant and give authors career resources and networks. Effective dissemination and outreach strategies are essential for publishing academic books in emerging fields. Innovative publishing models that use social media, online communities, and academic networks are supplementing library and academic institution-only distribution (Epstein, 2002; Einsohn & Schwartz, 2019; Rane et al., 2024c; Rane et al., 2024d). ResearchGate, Academia.edu, and LinkedIn are powerful tools for author networking, collaboration, and citations. Authors are also expected to interact with readers through blogs, webinars, and podcasts, making academic publishing a dynamic dialogue. Academic book publishing in emerging fields also depends on ethics. Intellectual property rights, data privacy, and inclusivity are becoming more important as innovation accelerates. title: Utilizing machine learning models for accurate crop prediction and yield optimization
abstract: Precision agriculture (PA) represents one of the most promising applications of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Internet of Things (IoT) technologies, and its practical implementations often rely on data collected from sensors such as weather stations, cameras, or leaf- and soil-sampling devices. Accurate prediction of crop yield is essential for agricultural producers, companies, and nations that are interested in food supply chain and agricultural planning, not just to optimize profit margins for producers but also to ensure adequate food security for the population. During the past three decades, machine learning models have become the primary way to address crop yield prediction tasks, owing to their efficient leveraging of large historical crop yield datasets in modeling complex nonlinear functions between exogenous factors and yield. In this paper, we examine this large body of literature on traditional and recently proposed machine learning techniques and how they succeed in predicting crop yield evaluated on different crops and countries.

title: Harvesting Intelligence: Data-Centric AI Approaches for Smarter Oilseed Production
abstract: Agriculture is crucial to the Indian economy, but population expansion poses a significant challenge to food security. This increase in demand for food necessitates farmers producing additional crops to meet this demand. Machine learning algorithms are utilized to forecast oilseed crop yields in several regions of Tamil Nadu to assist farmers in increasing crop yields. Actual yield data from 1961 to 2007 is used as a training set in this study and data from 2008 to 2019 is used as a validation set. In the first module, the suggested algorithm's accuracy is compared to that of Linear Regression, Support Vector Machine, Naive Bayes, and k-Nearest Neighbor methods and it achieves 90.19%, 86.26%, 80.71%, and 74.76% respectively. The linear regression algorithm is shown to be the best. The study involves the utilization of a linear regression algorithm in a recommendation system tailored for farmers. This system assists in making decisions about which crop to cultivate in a particular region at a specified time, achieving and it has an accuracy rate of 89.5%. In second module, it reveals how crop production is influenced by the type and quantity of fertilizers applied. To address this issue, the machine learning approaches are used to forecast agricultural output using inorganic fertilizers, as well as the amount and type of fertilizers to be used for oilseed crops in various districts of Tamil Nadu. The suggested technique outperforms conventional machine learning algorithms such as Random Forest, Linear Regression, Support Vector Machine, and Naive Bayes, with the accuracy rates of 93.17%, 91.22%, 86.47%, and 82.81%, respectively. For crop yield prediction, the random forest method outperforms other algorithms, although the decision tree approach works better for recommendation systems. The study provides farmers with a suggestion system to grow which crop and what type and quantity of inorganic fertilizers to be used in a certain location at a particular season. The recommendation system employs a Decision Tree Classifier to offer guidance on inorganic fertilizers selection for farmers, achieving a commendable accuracy rate of 92.6%. In third module, the accuracy of the proposed approach is compared to that of various machine learning techniques such as Bagging Ensemble, Random Forest, Linear Regression, and Naive bayes, which have accuracy rates of 94.5%, 93.5%, 91.5%, and 86.70%, respectively for organic manures application and yield prediction of oilseed crops. For agricultural yield prediction, the bagging algorithm outperforms other algorithms, whereas Gradient Boosting techniques outperform for recommendation systems with an accuracy rate of 93.1%. The study provides farmers with a suggestion system for determining which crop to grow, what type and quantity of organic manures to be applied and when to plant it. The fourth module describes that the success of oilseed crop production greatly depends on the use of Integrated Nutrient Management (INM) techniques. However, determining the optimal INM approach for specific conditions requires the expertise of professionals. A recommendation system for farmers is proposed in this study to assist them in selecting the best INM method for better yield and quality of oilseed crops. To select the optimum INM approach for a given set of votes, the system incorporates machine learning techniques such as Soft Voting Ensemble Algorithm (SVEA) which contains Soft Voting-based Ensemble Classifier with weights (SVECWW), and without weights (SVECWOW). In terms of accuracy and overall performance, the suggested system model beats all other proposed algorithms. A Stacked Generalization Ensemble Model (GUI) offers farmers with a user-friendly interface for extracting information such as soil parameters, crop kind, and climate conditions, and then proposes the optimum INM method based on that information. The system used real yield data achieving accuracy rates of 97.25%, 96.9%, and 68.72% for SVECWW, SVECWOW and, K-means respectively. The recommendation system utilizes a Stacking Generalization Ensemble model to facilitate integrated nutrients suggestions to farmers, delivering an impressive accuracy rate of 97.82%. In this study, a comprehensive evaluation was conducted, comparing the proposed algorithms with existing counterparts in all four modules. The results revealed that the performance of the proposed algorithms surpassed that of the existing ones. The research shows that employing machine learning algorithms to optimize INM techniques for oilseed crops in Tamil Nadu assist farmers improve crop yield, quality and lowers production costs and environmental consequences. Overall, the model's performance is assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, f-measure, and specificity metrics to determine whether the model performs as accurately as feasible.

title: Growing A Greener Future: Sustainable Practices in Agriculture
abstract: The global efforts towards ensuring that there is a balance between food production, environment, and the social well-being have based their efforts on sustainable agriculture. The traditional farming practices are increasingly proving to be ineffective in fulfilling future needs in a time that is marked by population explosion, scarcity of facts and climate change. It offers an all-inclusive answer which focuses on the Economical Closure, Ethical Conscience, and the Eco-Harmony. It is based on the philosophy that agriculture can be productive and regenerative and thus fulfilling human needs without threatening the natural ecosystems that support life.A new generation of ecological and technological innovations is transforming the production, processing and distribution of food. New and emerging agricultural practices like precision agriculture, agroforestry, vertical farming and organic farming and regenerative soil management are changing the rural and urban terrain. The innovations are productive and do not affect the environment significantly as they use data analytics, renewable energy, and recycling of refuses. Smart sensors and satellite mapping, such as enable producers to see what is happening to the soil, water use and adjust it in real time to increase crop production and minimize wastage. Together, the practices reflect a transformation towards resilience-farming that conserves biodiversity and ensures fair livelihoods and adjustment to changing climates.Chapter 1 introduces into the limelight the fact that India has immense problems in the world agricultural sector with almost 70 percent of its population dependent on the agricultural sector to make a living. The proportion of the industry in the national GDP is only 18, which is explained by the factors of the lack of mechanization and the lack of automation application. The history of agriculture development as far back as it has existed to the present day, through various forms is a critical transformation, with the transitioning of early methods to contemporary Smart farming (Agriculture 4.0). The physical, digital and biological worlds are merged here and work together with technologies, such as IoT, AI, analytics of Big Data, cloud computing, automation and robotics. Smart agriculture in India focuses on efficient utilization of resources, increase in productivity, enhance sustainability and quality and safety food.Agriculture 4.0 refers to the digital revolution which integrates IoT, Big Data analytics, and AI to enhance the productivity, efficiency and sustainability in agricultural sector. It entails innovative technologies such as IoT, wireless sensor networks, and AI to monitor crops and manage their diseases as well as optimizing their resources. Nonetheless, there are security and privacy issues. The IoT technology provides the opportunity to monitor the environment in real-time, AI and machine learning enhance the monitoring of crops and prediction of their yields. Edges computing, drone technologies, and remote sensing can contribute to real-time surveillance, and the lack of latency and network challenges. Smart agriculture has many advantages among them are enhanced productivity, economic sustainability and environmental sustainability. Nevertheless, there still are obstacles like issues related to security and privacy.In chapter 2, the author explains that farmers have started to apply nanotechnology to sustainable solutions in agriculture such as the use of smart delivery systems to deliver nutrients to crops, nano pesticides, nano fertilizers, and nano sensors to monitor agricultural parameters. The technologies are capable of enhancing the efficiency of the nutrients, crop production, and lessen wastage. Nanomaterials may be designed to express certain chemical groups and this improves plant health, tracking malnutrition and detection of pathogens. Examples are nano fertilizers, nano pesticides, plant growth regulators, soil enhancement, nutrient management, protection of phytopathogens and precision farming. Nanotechnology has many benefits over traditional pesticides and herbicides including low toxicity, high solubility and stability. It also helps in cleaning of soil and water by eliminating elements of harmful metals and organic wastes in wastewater. Nanotechnology however poses threats and issues to environmental and health safety necessitating new regulation frameworks, and the societal perceptions of its safety. DNA nanostructures, self-healing coats, plant nano-bionics or other bring about future prospects of increasing efficiency, efficacy, sustainability and precision in agriculture industry.Chapter 3 shed light on the Integrated Pest Management (IPM), an intensive pest control strategy that allows healthy production of crops by using preventive and curative strategies in an attempt to diminish dependence on toxic pesticides. It is founded on four principles prevention and suppression, monitoring, less use of pesticides and evaluation. Prevention entails setting up cropping mechanisms which have low chances of developing severe cases of pests whereas suppression seeks to mitigate the population of pests and their effects. Timely and informed pest control decisions can only be achieved through monitoring, keeping a check on the pest dynamics, and prediction pest control system can be used in anticipating a pest outbreak. One of the fundamental goals is to reduce the use of pesticides and the effectiveness and sustainability of IPM measures is evaluated. Pest control methodologies must be based on mechanical and physical means, and a key pillar is on biological control. IPM has already proved to be effective in Bangladesh and India and has had a huge success in lowering infection rates of pests and decreasing the use of fungicides and insecticides. The IPM programs use a variety of tools and methods to monitor and perform surveillance. In fruits, IPM provides an ecologically friendly and sustainable alternative, which combines the control of canopy, improved ventilation of tunnels, biocontrol agents and selective fungiciders applied to specific thresholds. In cereal crop, IPM focuses on monitoring of pests, using cultural and biological control and using pesticides when it becomes necessary.Chapter 4 leads us to the consideration of substitutes of chemical pesticides, one of the key being biological disease suppression. Vermicomposting is a biotechnology bioprocess which transforms organic waste into soil fertilizer, enhancing the soil fertility and it has particular qualities that results to the inhibition of pathogen in the plant. The fertile environment in the earthworm gut and associative microbes provides nutrients to foods and valuable microorganisms that may directly and indirectly inhibit pathogens. Vermicompost's inhibitory effects are due to a combination of biological and physicochemical processes. These biological processes are competitive exclusion, antibiosis and induced systemic resistance (ISR). Physicochemical processes involve enhanced health of the soils, healthy balance of nutrients and reduced prevalence of certain pathogens such as Pythium and Rhizoctonia solani, which are known to cause diseases in crops.The effectiveness of vermicompost has been established in diverse other agricultural systems such as the vegetables crops, fruit crops and rare agricultural field crops. There are, however, shortcomings including quality variability with unstable feed stocks, earthworm species as well as processing parameters, and the possibility of vermicompost becoming a source of antibiotic resistance gene.Chapter 5 discusses the Artificial intelligence (AI) which revolutionized agriculture by imitating human processes and enhancing different processes in the industry. AI algorithms can forecast production, reduce the effect of the environment, improve the safety of workers, reduce food prices and leverage food yield. Agricultural forces such as weather condition, price of inputs, soil erosion, crop losses, pest infestation, and climatic changes affect agriculture. AI is necessary to keep a check on agriculture such as monitoring soil, crops, diseases and pests. Soil management entails processes, procedures and treatments of soil aimed to enhance the soil. Traditional soil survey systems are employed to find out the pollutant of soil in urban center and compost and manure additions enhances soil aggregation and porousness. The fuzzy logic within soil management can be used to detect the carbon supply and demand through AI in different areas. The fuzzy logic of AI is applied in decision support systems (DSS) to detect random danger and soil quality and contamination.The big data technology in crop monitoring is applied to further develop seed selection and remote sensing to generate crop matrices. A device such as Arduino and Raspberry Pi 3 is automated, and implies and uses sensors in measuring soil moisture and water levels. To enable farmers to follow changes in the weather, AI-driven forecasting technology assists them.Chapter 6 summarizes pest monitoring is an important part of Integrated Pest Management (IPM) programs, which allows early detection of pest populations, and their dynamics. Innovations such as pheromone traps, light traps, colored sticky traps, pitfall traps, and suction traps aid in gathering information to apply in ecological observations, insects movement, timing of pest arrival, field surveying, pesticide application timing, biofixes, and forecasting new generations. Pest forecasting is necessary because it gives early warning, assists in the control efforts and minimizes cultivation expenses. Frequent surveys and monitoring help in a timely detection of pest populations, and their dynamics. The trap system based on AI will identify the major pest species in real-time and aid in targeted interventions. The modern pest forecasting models combine sensor collected data, weather prediction and crop models to forecast pest outbreak and propagation. Surveillance through sensors develops an ongoing feedback loop in making adaptive decisions. Instead of the simplistic advice suggested by an Entomologist, the current trends in IPM involve using integrated systems, also referred to as Decision Support Systems (DSS) that can provide real-time adaptive pest management guidance.Chapter 7 examines the importance of herbicides in managing plant life, and pests in the enduring farming. In intensive farming, herbicides are applied in efforts to fight weeds and various herbicides have diverse impacts on various crops. These materials are theoretically studied using the program WinXCom which gives the basic radiation interaction parameter of mass attenuation coefficient (muM). The test applies the X-rays or gamma photon to detect contaminated farming materials. Mass attenuation coefficient (MU) plays a key role in the identification and description of the materials to be used in herbicides in different crops and vegetables. Mass attenuation coefficients of different herbicides such as; 2, 4, 5-trichlorophenoxyacetic acid herbicide were determined using the WinXCom program.. It was found that the value of MFP and HVL rises with the rise of gamma photon energy to rise with precise pattern with the other herbicides in the range of energies. The researchers present significant details on how gamma ray shielding can be used in nuclear physics, and in agriculture. It also seeks to draw the line between regular and contaminated herbicides that could also be ineffectively used, like during the Vietnam War.The chapter 8 highlights the biosecurity in livestock production involving practices and technologies designed to prevent, detect, and respond to infectious disease impacting both livestock and humans. Traditional biosecurity measures have limitations, notably during major outbreaks like foot-and-mouth disease. Emerging technologies, particularly wearable biosensors, enhance early disease detection and health monitoring by providing real-time data on vital signs and behaviors. Machine learning models analyze this data, enabling anticipatory responses to health anomalies. Advanced tracking technologies and blockchain enhance traceability across supply chains, facilitating rapid response to outbreaks. However, challenges such as battery life, sensor durability, and high implementation costs remain. To advance biosecurity, systems architecture should integrate sensing, processing, connectivity, and governance layers while ensuring ethical and inclusive practices that consider the needs of smallholders and the privacy of sensitive data. Effective management of these technologies can significantly improve disease detection and mitigate zoonotic risks.Chapter 9 sheds light on Fuzzy logic, introduced by Lotfi A. Zadeh in 1965, addresses the uncertainty and imprecision of factors in agriculture, such as weather conditions, soil moisture, pest attacks, and crop growth. It is widely used in crop management, irrigation scheduling, and pest and disease prediction. Fuzzy logic helps in modeling linguistic terms like high temperature, low humidity, and moderate temperature, allowing for more efficient resource allocation and improved productivity. It reduces water and energy use, supports better agriculture and automation, reduces crop stress, and adapts to changing conditions for better crop yield. Fuzzy inference systems help judge risk levels and control actions based on uncertain conditions, reducing unnecessary use of chemicals, minimizing pesticide costs, and supporting sustainable farming practices. A case study in India demonstrates the effectiveness of a fuzzy logic-based irrigation system in reducing water consumption, increasing crop yield, and reducing stress and soil degradation. Future trends include more intelligent and data-driven irrigation scheduling, renewable energy-based irrigation, and models responsive to climate change.Chapter 10 highlights the Green Revolution revolutionized agriculture and dependency on hazardous chemicals like synthetic fertilizers, pesticides, and herbicides. These chemicals have harmful effects, including pest resistance, soil and water contamination, health risks, and ecosystem disruption. Indigenous Technical Knowledge (ITK) is a unique, inter-generational wisdom developed by indigenous peoples over millennia, enabling eco-friendly livelihood activities. Integrating ITK with modern IPM practices offers a promising pathway towards sustainable and culturally grounded pest management. Advantages of integrating ITK include cultural preservation, environmental and public health benefits, enhanced sustainability, increased resilience, and cost-effectiveness. Traditional practices, such as crop rotation and transgenic technology, can also be used to manage pests. Biological control using natural enemies offers environmentally safe and sustainable options for managing insect pests and plant pathogens in agriculture.The cultivation of responsibility and foresight is the ultimate objective of sustainable agriculture, rather than merely the cultivation of commodities. Societies can guarantee that agricultural expansion does not result in environmental degradation by adopting both innovative and traditional methods. Investing in sustainable farming today is an investment in the future stability of generations, environmental health, and food security. Chapter 11 focuses on Insect bioconversion plays a crucial role in the circular bioeconomy, transforming food and agro-industrial waste into valuable products like protein feed, biofertilizers, and bioactive compounds. Insects such as the black soldier fly (Hermetia illucens), mealworm (Tenebrio molitor), and housefly (Musca domestica) effectively convert a range of organic residues, contributing to sustainable waste management by reducing waste volume and greenhouse gas emissions. This chapter explores the biological and technological mechanisms behind insect-mediated waste transformation, highlighting the importance of gut microbiota in nutrient assimilation and pathogen suppression. Despite potential benefits, challenges like regulatory constraints, safety concerns, and feedstock variability hinder large-scale adoption. Addressing these barriers through innovation and policy standardization is essential for realizing the full potential of insect biorefineries, which can enhance environmental sustainability and resource efficiency in agriculture.
